title: Why user story mapping
description: What user story mapping changes for product, engineering, design, leadership and founders, and how it helps a team deliver impactful work faster.
text: It empowers you and your team to deliver impactful work faster than ever. User story mapping drives collaboration, discovery, insight, and ruthless prioritisation. It requires everyone involved to shape the project, understand its objectives, and share in its impact. It strengthens cross-department relationships, saves time, reduces waste, and helps you release faster. Product. You're no longer the only one holding the plan. Instead of writing the requirements first and walking everyone through them, you lead the planning session where you and the team map the product. Everyone leaves knowing what comes first and why, motivated because they have a stake in it. When it's time to write tickets, you and the team start from the tasks on the story map. The story map stays in use from that first meeting right the way through, evolving along with the product. Engineering. No more being brought in once the big decisions are made. You're in the room when the product is mapped, so you can flag what's risky, or cheaper another way, before anything is promised. When it's time to write tickets, you and the product team start from the tasks on the story map, and each release slice says what that release needs. Once it's agreed, the work is focused, minimising scope creep. Because you can see the whole journey, today's choices won't box you in later. You helped make the trade-offs, so you know why your work matters. Design. There's no need to design the whole product before anyone has used any of it. You're in the room when the journey is mapped, so what you know about users shapes the plan from the start. Each release slice shows you and the product team which steps to design next, and because you can see the whole journey, they still join up into one experience. Flows months away can wait until people have used what you shipped. With the slice agreed, you design what's in it, not everything that might come later. Leadership. A plan the team builds together is one everyone supports. People who helped shape the plan feel empowered to act on it and motivated to deliver it. You can see the whole product in one place: what each release is for, what's in it and how far along it is, without chasing status updates. What people know ends up on the story map for everyone to see. When priorities change, you can see what moves before anyone commits to it. Founders. The product no longer lives only in your head. Mapping it lays the whole idea out where your team, contractors and investors can see it. The first release slice shows the smallest thing worth launching, so you spend your time and money proving the idea, not building everything at once. As you learn from customers, the story map changes with you, and everyone you bring on can see where the product is going and why.

title: How do you decide what to build?
description: Scrum and Kanban assume there's already a backlog, and say little about where it comes from. What fills that gap today.
text: Agile is great at helping you build things. Short cycles, working software, and room to change course as you learn. But the two methods most teams mean when they say "agile", Scrum and Kanban, both assume there's already a backlog of work. Agile needs a backlog to get going. It doesn't say where a good one comes from. That's the gap. This page looks at what fills it today. Scrum starts with a Product Owner and a product backlog. The Scrum Guide says the Product Owner sets the Product Goal and orders the backlog, but not how the goal or the first backlog come about. That's deliberate: the guide calls Scrum "purposefully incomplete". Plenty of teams run a "Sprint 0" first, but it isn't in the guide, and it's usually spent choosing the tech stack and setting up, not deciding what to build. Kanban manages the flow of work that already exists. One of its core principles is "start with what you do now", so choosing the work sits outside it. The Agile Manifesto values working software, collaborating with customers and responding to change. It doesn't say how to choose what to build in the first place. Some agile frameworks do plan up front. XP starts with an Exploration phase, DSDM has Feasibility and Foundations, and Disciplined Agile has Inception. Even these assume someone has already chosen the idea. They refine an idea rather than find one. And they're not what most teams run day to day. It varies a lot from team to team, but it usually goes like this: Ideas come in from everywhere. Customers, support, sales, analytics, leadership and the team itself. The product manager frames and ranks them. Raw requests become problems worth solving, often on a Now, Next, Later roadmap. Discovery tests the big ones. Interviews, prototypes and spikes check an idea holds up before anyone commits to it. Someone writes it up. A product brief, a hypothesis, a requirements document or a pitch: the problem, who has it, what success looks like and what's out of scope. The write-up becomes a backlog. Epics, user stories and acceptance criteria, refined until they're ready for a sprint. Then Scrum or Kanban takes over. Busy teams often jump straight from step 1 to step 5. A stakeholder asks for something, the Product Owner writes a ticket, and it goes into the next sprint. Bigger companies lean the other way, with long documents and sign-offs. Either way, all five steps happen outside the framework, and the delivery team often sees only the result: the backlog. Most projects fill the gap with a document, then a list of tickets. The problem with big documents and long lists looks at what goes wrong there, and what a story map does instead. A story map can help you decide what to build, even before there's an idea. How a story map helps teams decide what to build shows how.

title: The problem with big documents and long lists
description: Why a long document and a list of tickets lose the shape of a product, and what a story map does instead.

headings.text: Problem 2: The list with no story

text: Most software projects start with an idea, and then the idea becomes a document, usually a big one. It goes by different names: technical specification, product requirements document (PRD), functional spec, business requirements document (BRD), or even the "Project Phoenix" doc. Whatever it's called, it's typically written by one or two people, either a business analyst or product manager. From there, it's enhanced with design mockups and eventually distilled into a backlog of tickets. This page looks at the problems with that process. The people who write the document put days into it: what the product should do, who it's for, the acceptance criteria, the business case and how success will be measured. Most of the team will read it, but each person comes away with their own mental picture of the product. That's usually where things start to go wrong. Here are a few examples of how written requirements can sometimes be interpreted differently to how the writer intended. Someone once ordered a leaving cake that said "Best Wishes Suzanne" and, underneath that, "We will miss you". Someone else read those requirements. The result: Photo from Cake Wrecks, the blog by Jen Yates. This cake started the blog and is on the cover of the Cake Wrecks book. Someone else wrote on a graduation cake order that they wanted sprinkles. The baker read those requirements too. The result: Photo from the Cake Wrecks post. A mum-to-be was having triplets, so the order asked for "Congratulations" to be written on the cake three times. The result: Photo from the Cake Wrecks post. A birthday cake order came with a note for the bakery: nuts allergy. The result: Photo from the Cake Wrecks post. All four bakeries read the words exactly as they were written. The writers intended them to be interpreted differently. I mean, they were clear requirements, right? A long software project document does the same thing on a bigger scale. A typical project document can run to tens of pages, sometimes hundreds, covering many topics for different audiences, at varying levels of detail. Everyone is asked to review it, to confirm its correctness, and usually, after some of them have read it, it's finalised and approved by everyone. Example: Coffee App Product Requirements 50 pages, read and approved by four teams. Did they all really read it and understand it? The truth is, people read documents in different ways. Some skim. Some read half, feel they have the idea, and move on. Others read it over in a few sittings. The approvals hide the differences. Design pictures one app, engineering visualises another, management expects a third, and the gaps turn up once the work starts. The research backs this up: Same words, different meanings. 104 software practitioners read the same 12 "if/then" requirements and disagreed about what they meant, even when they knew how the system behaved. Writers overestimate how clear they are. In a study of email, senders expected 78% of readers to tell whether their message was serious or sarcastic. Only 56% could. Long documents get skipped. In a study of terms of service, 98% of students agreed to them ==without noticing a clause that handed over their first-born child!== The project document starts as the reference, but over time people check it less often, and the tickets take over. Sooner or later, the document becomes a backlog of tickets. Here's the backlog for our example coffee ordering app. Seventeen tickets, in the order they were written. Try answering these questions from the list of tickets: In what order will a customer use these? How many sprints until a customer can order a coffee? What's missing? (Something is.) It's hard. This is a typical backlog for a new project: the document boiled down into things to build, from user requirements to good ideas. The list says what to build, not where each piece fits or how the pieces add up to something people can use. Sorting it by priority doesn't help much. It changes the order, not the picture. Jeff Patton came up with user story mapping because a flat backlog can't show how a product fits together. Of flattening the plan into a list, he wrote: "we pull all the leaves off the tree and load them into a leaf bag – then cut down the tree." (The new user story backlog is a map, Jeff Patton.) A story map keeps the tree: the team maps the journey together, spots the gaps, and slices out a first release that works from start to finish. The backlog comes straight from the story map, already in order. A story map puts the same work on one page, as a story anyone can read in a couple of minutes. The team builds it together, so different pictures of the product come out in the conversation, before the work starts. Over the next section, you'll see this backlog turn into one, and these questions get answered. User story mapping was created by Jeff Patton, who wrote the book on it, User Story Mapping. There's more on his site.

title: Lay out the user journey in a story map
description: A story map starts with who the product is for and the steps they take, from left to right.
text: A user story map starts with people, not tickets. Who is the software for, and what are they trying to do? For the coffee app, that's a customer who wants to order a coffee. Ordering a coffee takes a few steps: browse the menu, customise a drink, add it to the cart, pay, then confirm the order. Put those along the top, in order, and each ticket goes under the step it belongs to. Tickets from the backlog, under the steps of ordering a coffee. The rows along the top have names: Users are who the product is for. Activities are what they're trying to do. Steps are how they do it, from left to right. Together, they're the backbone of the story map. Read it from left to right and it tells the story of the product: the customer browses the menu, customises a drink, adds it to the cart, pays and confirms the order. Then what? The story stops once the order is in. There's no step for collecting the coffee, and no way of knowing when it's ready. A whole step is missing. In the list, that gap was invisible. On the story map, it's an empty space you can't miss.

title: Prioritise work in a story map
description: The work under each step, ordered by what matters most, and the gaps a story map shows.
text: Under each green step, the Yellow cards are tasks: the work needed to let a user complete that step. Here they're the tickets from our backlog, and now you can see where each one belongs. On other story maps, a task might be a bigger piece of work, like an epic, and span multiple tickets. Within each column, the order matters. The most important task goes at the top, and the nice-to-haves further down. The same story map, with the most important task at the top of each column. To sort a column, ask: if the customer could only have one of these, which would it be? Most people pay with their phone in a coffee app, so Apple Pay / Google Pay goes above Credit card. The missing step from the last page is in place now too: Collect Order, with Notify when ready under it. That gives the story map two directions. Left to right is the order things happen. Top to bottom is how much they matter. The next page uses both to pick a first release.

title: Slice an MVP with a story map
description: Two ways to pick a first release, and why a thin slice across the whole journey works best.
text: You can't build everything at once, so you need a first release. There are two ways to pick one. The first is one step at a time: finish browsing, then customising, then the cart, and so on. One step at a time is how engineers often plan the work, since each part gets finished properly. After the first release, customers can browse the whole menu and can't order anything. The second is release slicing: go through the steps from left to right and ask what's the minimum implementation each one needs to work and be useful. Take only the tasks that cover it, so users can get from the first step to the last in the simplest way that works. Release slicing. Customers can order and pay for a coffee from the first release. We get a working product that can validate our assumptions much earlier. Also, good ideas like additional payment methods and additional drinks options come in a later slice. On a story map, a slice is a row across every step that groups tasks into a release. The first is often called the MVP, the minimum viable product: the smallest version that's still useful. Everything else waits in a later slice. Thin slices get something real in front of people sooner. A coffee app that only lets you browse items is a menu. One that lets you order a plain coffee is a new revenue stream. You can also see what its first customers order, where they give up and what they ask for, which shows you what to build next. Experience tells us that not all of our ideas are good, and not everything we build gets used. So instead of trying to predict what will succeed, focus on testing assumptions quickly and cheaply. Getting something out sooner shows us what works before we spend too long on the wrong thing, and if we have to throw something away, it hasn't cost much.

title: How a story map helps teams decide what to build
description: Find the problems worth fixing with a now story map, test ideas with research and prototypes, shape them with a future story map, and slice to decide what to build first.

headings.text: Bring in what you already know

text: A user story map can start before there's an idea. The team maps how things work today, finds the problems worth fixing, and tests ideas before committing to them. By the time the plan is agreed, everyone has seen why. A now story map lays out how something works today. Walk the journey with the people who do it every day, step by step, including the workarounds. Then mark the problems or pain points under the step where they happen, in a colour of their own. A workaround, such as a shortcut only a few people know or a requirement to look up critical data elsewhere, is a missing feature, so give each one a card. People working around the product aren't misusing it, they're showing what it's missing. The steps where problems pile up are the place to look first. A step with five problems under it says more than a list of complaints, because everyone can see where in the journey each one happens, and what comes before and after it. Ideas come up as soon as people see the problems laid out. Put each one under the step it would improve, in its own colour. An idea next to the problem it fixes is easier to weigh up than one on a list. Interviews, support requests and usage data all fit on the story map. Put each finding under the step it's about. A problem that turns up in interviews and in the data deserves more attention than one that turns up once. Anything nobody can answer yet goes on as a question to follow up. A future story map shapes the idea. Copy the now story map, keep the steps that still make sense, change the ones that don't, and turn the opportunities worth taking into tasks. Some ideas only show their problems once people try them. Build a quick prototype of one slice, show it to the people who'll use it, and change the story map with what you learn. Build with AI turns a slice into a working prototype, so trying an idea costs little. Slice an MVP: take the smallest set of tasks that gets someone through the whole journey, and give the slice a goal. The goal says which problems the release fixes, so anyone can trace the decision back to the now story map. If there's already a write-up, bring it along and map from it. If there isn't, you don't need one: the team works out what to build and why as they map. Either way, the story map turns that into an ordered, sliced plan the whole team can start on.

title: How story mapping changes a product team
description: What a team gets from a story map, and how it changes the way work goes from an idea to a release.
text: That's how a story map works: people and their journey along the top, tasks underneath with the most important first, and slices across for releases. Here's what a team gets from using user story mapping: The whole product at once. Anyone can read the product story from left to right, in one place, without digging through lists of tickets or reading long documents for context. Gaps show up early. An empty step is hard to miss, so missing work turns up before it's built, not after. Releases that work. Slicing across the journey means each release works from start to finish. A shared picture. When a team builds the story map together, everyone leaves with the same idea of the product. Teams usually make a story map at the start of something new, then come back to it to plan the next release or to see how one is going. A story map also changes how work gets from an idea to a release. Here's a typical agile flow without one, next to the same flow with one. Without a story map, the backlog comes from the document. With one, the team builds it together from the journey, and comes back to it after every release. The story map comes first, and the backlog is built from it. Everything after that follows the slices, so each sprint works towards building a working journey rather than separate parts. In user story mapping, the first step isn't a document. It's discussing the opportunity together: who it's for and why it's worth building. That can be a conversation or a one-page brief. If your organisation already has a project document, use it as a reference while you map. It changes design too. Designers work on the steps in the next slice, when they're needed. Flows that won't be built for months can wait, since they may change once people use the product and give feedback. A story map doesn't replace your issue tracker or your roadmap. The tickets still live in the tracker, usually with much more granular detail than a story map card, and the roadmap says when things ship. The story map shows how they fit together and can link to tickets and release dates if needed, but that's really more a convenience than a rule. Agile ways of working, like Scrum and Kanban, are great at showing what you're building right now. They're not as good at showing how it connects to everything else. Long-running projects often follow the same pattern: they start with energy, a vision and a shared document, and six months later that document has been replaced by a giant backlog. Everyone knows their own tickets, but no single place shows how the work fits together as a product. The vision isn't lost because people forgot it. It's lost because nothing in the process preserves it. User story mapping is the missing practice that preserves it. The story map keeps it in one place the whole team can see, from the first conversation to the latest release. If a sprint shows you a tree, a story map shows you the forest. You now know enough about user story maps to try building one. Create a user story map starts one in the app, and Run a user story mapping session builds the first one with your team.

title: What is a user story map?
description: A story map lays out a product as the journey people take through it, with the work for each release in slices across it.

headings.text: The parts of a story map

text: A story map lays out a product as the journey people take through it. Instead of a long backlog, it shows the whole product on one page: who it's for, what they do, the work behind each step, and which parts you're building first. Users are the people the product is for. Activities are the big things they're trying to do. Steps break the journey down, from left to right. Users, activities and steps together are the backbone of the story map. Tasks are the Yellow cards under each step, with the most important at the top. They're the work that lets someone do that step, from a single ticket to a bigger piece like an epic. Slices run across the story map and group the tasks into releases. The first is often the MVP: a thin slice with the minimum implementation each step needs to work and be useful, so users can get from the first step to the last in the simplest way that works. A story map shows the whole product in one place, brings gaps to light early, gives you releases that work from start to finish, and leaves the team with a shared picture of what you're building. How story mapping changes a product team goes through each of these, and shows where a story map fits in the way you work. A story map can also show how a process works or the technical work behind a feature. Jeff Patton came up with user story mapping, and wrote about it in his book User Story Mapping. There's more on his site. Agile has a gap explains the problem a story map solves, and How story mapping works follows one backlog as it becomes a story map. Create a user story map then starts one of your own in the app. To build one online with your team, What is a story mapping tool? covers what the software does and what to look for.

title: What is a story mapping tool?
description: A story mapping tool is software for building a user story map online with your team. What one does, and what to look for in user story mapping software.

headings.text: What a story mapping tool does
Sticky notes, whiteboards and story mapping software
What to look for in a user story mapping tool

text: A story mapping tool is software for building a user story map online. The team lays out the journey, adds the work under each step and slices it into releases, in one place that everyone can open and change. What is a user story map? covers the story map itself. A story map has a set shape: steps run from left to right, tasks sit under each step, and slices run across them. A story mapping tool is built around that shape: Every task sits under a step and in a slice, so the columns and rows stay lined up. Moving a step brings its tasks with it. Several people can work on the same story map at once. Each task can hold its own detail, such as a body, a status, points and tags. The work can go on to the tracker the team already uses. A story map works in any of them, so pick what suits the team. Sticky notes on a wall suit a team in one room. Everyone can stand at the wall, move the notes around and talk it through. An online whiteboard brings people in different places together on one board. Story mapping software is built around the shape of a story map. The whole team edits it live from one link, each release shows its goal, date and progress, and the cards can go to your tracker or to an AI tool to build from. Many teams map on a wall first, then move the story map into a tool to plan each release from it. Slices for releases, each with a goal and a date. Live editing, so everyone sees changes as they happen. Quick invites, so everyone in the session can join from one link, with no account to create first. Progress, with a status and points on the cards. A link to your tracker, so cards don't need copying across by hand. Structured data behind every story map, in standard formats such as YAML, so AI tools and scripts can read it, and you can move it to another tool. Backups and locks, to record progress, undo accidental changes and hold an agreed plan. Storymaps.io is a story mapping tool that runs in the browser, with no sign-up needed, no paywall and no trials. Click Start Mapping on the home page and share the link with the team. Plan releases with story map slices covers releases, goals and dates. Edit a story map together covers working live. Review release progress on a story map covers status and points. Jira, Asana, Phabricator and Linear integrations cover sending cards to a tracker. Export a story map covers JSON, YAML and CSV files. Story map data links give the data behind any story map, always up to date, and the Storymaps CLI edits it as YAML from the terminal. Back up and restore a story map records progress with a note at each milestone, and restores an earlier version if something is changed by accident. Lock a story map keeps an agreed plan exactly as it is, until it's ready to be worked on at the next session. Start a story map project covers grouping story maps as tabs. Build with AI turns a slice into a working prototype, so product teams can build to learn.

title: Run a user story mapping session
description: Build the first story map together as a team. Who to invite, how to set up, and the order to map in, from the users to a first release.
text: The first story map works best when the team builds it together. Everyone adds what they know, and everyone leaves with the same picture of the product and a first release they agreed on. New to story maps? What is a user story map? explains the parts. Invite the people who'll shape and build the product: Product, to lead the session and set out the goal. Engineering, to say what's feasible, and flag what's risky or cheaper another way. Design, to share what they've learned about users and shape the experience. Key stakeholders, such as the sponsor or a department head, to agree the goal and back the first release. Anyone close to the users, such as support or sales, to say what users ask for and struggle with. Bring a short brief if there is one: who the product is for and why it's worth building. How story mapping changes a product team explains where a brief fits in. Create a user story map and name it. Copy the link from Share → Share URL and send it to everyone, so the whole team edits the same story map. Changes show for everyone as they happen. The first time someone arrives, the app asks for their name, so everyone can see who's who. How you run it depends on where everyone is: In person: put the story map on the big screen, and everyone works on it from their own device. Remote: the person leading shares their screen, and everyone else works on it from their own device. If everyone's cursors moving around distract whoever's presenting, they can click Hide external cursors in the view controls at the bottom right. It only changes their own view. Change the story map view has more. Put questions on the story map as Lime cards, the legend's colour for questions, under the step they're about. Use the Notes tab for decisions and anything that doesn't belong to one step. Everyone with the link sees the same notes. Start with the users row. Name the people the product is for, such as Customer and Barista. Settle any disagreement here first, since everything else on the story map depends on who it's for. Lay out the backbone from left to right: the activities, then the steps under each. Tell it as the story of one user when everything goes right (the happy path): first they do this, then that. Keep it high-level for now, and get the whole journey down before anyone goes into detail on one step. Then read it back out loud, from left to right. If one step doesn't lead to the next, there's a step missing. Define the story map backbone shows how to add and move users, activities and steps. When someone raises something that could go wrong, or an unusual case, add it as a Rose card under that step, the legend's colour for edge cases, and keep going. Under each step, everyone adds the tasks they think are needed to complete it as Yellow cards, the legend's colour for tasks, and any good ideas for the future. Everyone can do this at the same time. Don't slice releases yet. To show what's for now and what's for later, move the tasks for now to the top of the column. With everyone adding at once, expect some repeats. Go through the story map together from left to right, one step at a time, and talk through what's there. Merge tasks that overlap, remove duplicates, and reword any task that isn't clear to everyone. If the group can't settle something yet, turn it into a Lime question card and move on. Then sort each column, with the most important task at the top. If someone moves a card and someone else moves it back, stop and talk about why. Add tasks to a story map covers adding and moving them. The conversation is as valuable as the story map. As Jeff Patton puts it: "Use the creation of the model as an opportunity to elicit discussion about the features being built." (It's All in How You Slice, Jeff Patton.) Decide the first release together. Go through the steps from left to right and ask what's the minimum implementation each one needs to work and be useful. Move the tasks that cover it into the first slice, so users can get from the first step to the last in the simplest way that works. Then give the slice a goal everyone agrees on, such as "Customers can order and pay ahead, then pick up their coffee", and a target date to make it real. Then deal with the rest. If the remaining work is already prioritised, slice it into later releases. If not, put it all in one Later slice to come back to. Nothing needs deleting. The session is done when the team agrees on the first slice, usually the MVP or V1, and who's picking up what next. Slice an MVP with a story map explains why the slice runs across the whole journey, and Plan releases with story map slices shows how to add one and give it a goal and a date. The story map is where the plan lives from now on: Mark the milestone with a backup, with a note such as "After the first session", so you can always get back to what the team agreed. Build the first slice as a prototype to learn from users before the team commits to it. Build with AI shows how. Turn the first slice into tickets with the team. The Jira, Asana, Phabricator and Linear integrations can send the cards as epics or tasks, to save copying them across by hand. Share the link wherever the team talks about the work, such as a chat or a ticket. Add new ideas and feedback as they come in, under the step they relate to, so they're there when you plan the next release. Come back to it to plan each release. See how a release is going in Review release progress on a story map. Tag each card with the team that will build it, such as mobile or payments, so each team can see its own work. Select the cards for one team, by dragging a box around them or with Shift+click. Click Tags on the toolbar, type the team name in New tag... and press Enter. Do the same for each team. To see the work for one team, click the funnel beside the search box, tick the tag under Tags and click Done. The cards for that team stay bright in every step and slice. Filters only change what you see, so each team can view its own work at the same time. Search and filter a story map covers the rest, including searching within the tagged cards.

title: Find your story maps
description: Every story map has its own link, and the link is the way back. Bookmark it, or open a story map from the recent list on the home page or in the main menu.
text: Every user story map has its own link, such as storymaps.io/abc12345, and the link is how you get back to it. When you name a story map, the app shows a one-time reminder to bookmark it, just below the name. Copy link copies the link, to keep somewhere safe or send to the team. Got it closes the reminder. Don't show again stops the reminder on every story map in this browser. Press Ctrl+D, or Cmd+D on a Mac, to bookmark the page. On a phone, add it from the browser menu. The app keeps a list of the story maps you've opened in this browser, newest first, with when you last opened each one. On the home page, click Open a recent map under Start Mapping. Inside a story map, open the main menu and choose Recent maps. The story map that's open shows as Open now. The browser Back button closes the list. A story map you opened inside a project shows as the project, with its number of story maps, and opens on the story map you last had open there. The list lives in this browser only, and is never sent anywhere. Another browser or device has its own list, so bookmark the story maps you want to keep. Click × on a row to take it off the list. Click Clear list to empty it. Neither deletes a story map. It still opens from its link. A story map that no longer exists leaves the list when you try to open it. Anyone with the link can open the story map, so the link is also how the team finds it. Copy it from Share → Share URL, and put it wherever the team talks about the work. Share a story map has more. Anyone with the link can edit the story map. If you're sharing it publicly, it's wise to lock it and create a backup, in case of unexpected changes.

title: Now story map
description: Map how things work today, then highlight the problems or pain points and the opportunities in their own colours, so the team agrees what to fix before anyone designs the fix.
text: A now story map, sometimes called an as-is story map, lays out how something works today, including the problems or pain points. Walk the current journey with the people who do it every day, then mark the problems. It's also the place to highlight opportunities. Ideas come up as soon as people see the problems laid out, so put each one on the story map, under the step it would improve. Everyone sees the same problems and the same opportunities, in the order a customer hits them. Pay close attention to workarounds. Each one is a missing feature, something people had to invent for themselves to get the job done, so give it a card as both a problem and an opportunity. Users are the people in the journey today, such as Customer and Barista. Steps are what really happens, in order, not what should happen. Cards under each step start with what happens today, then the problems, then the opportunities. Use colour to tell the cards apart. Task cards are Yellow to start with, and the other colours are yours to choose. Give each kind of card its own colour, and name it in the legend so everyone reads the story map the same way. The sample uses: Yellow for how it works today. Rose for problems. Lime for opportunities. Cyan for questions to follow up. The Overview counts each colour, so you can see at a glance where the problems pile up. Customise story map cards covers colours, and Review release progress on a story map covers the legend. Map it with the people who do the work every day. They know the workarounds that never made it into a process document. Before you redesign something that already exists. When a team inherits a product or a process and needs to understand it fast. To make the case for change, with the problems laid out where they happen. A now story map is the starting point for a future story map. Copy it with Menu → Copy this map, keep the steps that still make sense, and turn the opportunities into the tasks of a first release.

title: Future story map
description: The classic story map. Imagine the product people will use, lay out the journey, and slice it into releases that each work from start to finish.
text: A future story map is the classic kind: the product you're about to build, laid out as the journey people will take through it. It's what most people mean by a story map, and what the rest of these docs build. Users are the people the product is for. Activities and steps are the journey you want them to have. Tasks under each step are the work to build it, with the most important at the top. Slices cut the work into releases, starting with a thin MVP that works end to end. Give each slice a goal, and track the work with statuses and points as it gets built. Plan releases with story map slices and Review release progress on a story map cover both. Planning a new product, or a big new feature. Turning a brief or a requirements document into a backlog the whole team understands. Agreeing the first release with everyone in the room. Mapping a product that already exists? Start with a now story map, so the future one fixes real problems. How story mapping works walks through one of these from a backlog, and Run a user story mapping session shows how to build one as a team.

title: Technical story map
description: Map a system where the users are other systems, such as an app calling an API, with the calls as the steps and the engineering work under each.
text: The user doesn't have to be a person. In a technical story map the users are systems, such as a mobile app, a payment provider or a screen in the shop, and the steps are the calls they make. Engineering gets the same view of the work that product gets from a classic story map. Users are the systems that call yours, such as Mobile app and Payment provider. Activities are what each system is trying to do, such as Place an order. Steps are the calls, in the order one request makes them: GET /menu, POST /orders, then the webhook back. Tasks are the engineering work behind each call. Mark edge cases as Rose cards, the legend's colour for them, such as a webhook that arrives twice. Slice it the same way as any story map. The first slice gets one request working end to end. Later slices harden it: retries, rate limits, monitoring. Tag tasks by service or team, such as backend and payments. Search and filter a story map then shows one team its work across every slice. Designing an API, an integration or a data pipeline. Planning a migration, with the old and new systems as users. Showing product what the engineering work behind a feature really is. A technical story map works well next to the future story map of the same product. Start a story map project keeps them together as tabs.

title: Process story map
description: Map a process from start to finish, such as onboarding or offboarding, and use slices to show the different routes people take through it.
text: A process story map lays out how something gets done, step by step, such as onboarding a new starter or handling a refund. Slices show the different routes through it, so you can see where they split and what each one skips. Users are the people going through the process, such as New starter and Leaver. Activities are the big stages, such as Join the team and Leave the team. Steps are the individual things that happen, in order. Slices can show the routes, which is how we'd lay it out. The first slice is the standard route, and each slice under it is a variation, such as an experienced hire or a seasonal temp. Where a route does the same as the standard route, leave that column empty. Then the cards in each route are only what's different, and the gaps show what that route skips. Mark the problems in their own colour as you go, such as paper forms that go missing. A process story map soon shows where things fall through the cracks. Use a process story map to lay out how work gets done, rather than to plan a product. It's ideal for HR departments, because processes such as hiring, onboarding, leave and offboarding pass between HR, line managers, IT and the employee, and often change with the role, location or type of contract. A process story map puts every stage in one place and shows how each route differs. It works well for: Onboarding and offboarding, for staff or customers. Any process with variations, such as complaint handling, returns, refunds or approvals. Finding the handoffs where things get dropped. Once the problems are on the story map, make a future story map of the process you want instead. Menu → Copy this map gives you a copy to start from.

title: Define the story map backbone
description: Set out who the story map is for, what they're trying to do and the steps of their journey, in the three rows along the top.
text: The backbone is the three rows along the top of the user story map: users, activities and steps. It tells the story of the product from left to right, and everything else on the story map sits under it. Lay out the user journey in a story map explains why it runs that way. Users are the people the product is for, such as a customer or a barista. Click a user to rename it. + user under a user adds another in the same place, for people who start the journey together. To bring in a user further along the journey, such as the coffee shop that takes the order, click the dashed space in the Users row above that step. Activities are the big things users are trying to do, such as Order Coffee or Fulfil Orders. An activity sits above the step where it starts. To add one, click the dashed space in the Activities row above the step where it should start, and type its name. Steps break the journey into what a person does, from left to right, in the order they do it. Click the dashed space to the right of the last step to add a step, then click the new step to name it. Right-click a step to add a step before or after it, or to duplicate it. Name steps as things a person does, in a word or two: Browse Menu, Pay, Collect Order. Read the steps from left to right as a story. If the story skips something, such as collecting the coffee after paying, a step is missing. Drag a step by the ↔ at its top left to move it. Everything under it, in every slice, moves with it. To delete a step, right-click it and choose Delete column, or choose Delete Column from its … menu. Deleting a step takes the cards under it too, in every slice. Ctrl+Z brings them all back. A spacer column is an empty column between steps, which puts a gap in the journey. Use one to group steps, such as everything before and after an order is placed. Right-click a step and choose Add spacer column before or after.

title: Add tasks to a story map
description: Add tasks under each step, give them a title and detail, and move or delete them.
text: Tasks are the Yellow cards under each step: the work that lets someone do that step. A task can be a single ticket or a bigger piece of work, like an epic, and can link to the tickets in your tracker. A task sits in the column of the step it belongs to, and in the slice of the release it's planned for. Click + at the bottom of a column. The new task opens large, so you can type its title and add more detail in the body underneath. Close it with × or Esc. The title shows on the story map, and the body is there whenever you open the task again. Click a task's title on the story map to change it. Titles are short, up to 38 characters, so put the rest in the body. Hover over a task and click its ⤢ to open it large again. A task with a body shows a small mark, so you can tell it has more inside. Open a task's … menu for its colour, status, points, tags and link. In the large view, three buttons add a template to the body in one click: As a, I want, So that for a user story. Given, When, Then for a scenario. Acceptance criteria for a list of what must be true. Press Enter to move to the next line, and to start the next item in a list. Every task has its own link. Opening it opens the story map with that task open in the large view, which is handy in a chat message or a ticket. Right-click the task and choose Copy link to card. The task's … menu has it too, and so does the share button next to × when the task is open large. Users and activities have links too. You can copy a link from a locked story map, where the task opens read-only. Inside a project, the link keeps the project, so the tabs are there when it opens. Drag a task up or down its column, to another step, or into another slice. The story map scrolls as you drag near its edge. To move several at once, select them by dragging a box around them, starting from an empty part of the story map. Then drag any one of them. Open its … menu and choose Delete. To delete several, select them and click Delete in the toolbar that appears. Ctrl+Z undoes it. Put the most important tasks at the top of each column. When you slice the story map into releases, the top tasks usually go first. Prioritise work in a story map explains why.

title: Write user stories on a story map
description: Open a card large to write a title and body, and add a user story, a scenario or acceptance criteria in one click.
text: The title of a card is short, so the user story map stays readable. The body holds everything else: a user story, how it should behave, what has to be true for it to be done. Hover over a card and click its ⤢. A new task opens large on its own when you add it. The strip along the top shows the step and slice the card is in, and whether the slice is closed or complete. The title is under it, up to 38 characters. The body underneath can be as long as you need. The line at the bottom shows the card's status, points, tags and link. Click Edit to change them or pick a colour. A card with a body shows a small mark on the story map, so you can tell it has more inside. Close the large view with × or Esc. Three buttons add a template to the body in one click: As a, I want, So that adds a user story. Given, When, Then adds a scenario, for how the feature should behave. Acceptance criteria starts a list of what must be true for the story to be done. Fill in each line after the starter words. Enter moves to the next line to fill in, and in a list it starts the next item. Keep the title as the short name everyone uses for the task, and put the user story in the body. The story map stays easy to scan, and the detail is one click away.

title: Customise story map cards
description: Give cards a colour, a status, points, tags and a link, one card at a time or many at once.
text: Every card on the user story map can carry more than its title: a colour, a status, an estimate, tags and a link. They show along the bottom of the card, so the story map tells you more at a glance. Hover over a card and click its … to open its menu. Color picks one of 14 colours. Points is an estimate of size, in whatever units your team uses. Status is none, done, in progress, planned or blocked. Tags are free-text labels. As you type, tags already on the story map are offered. Add URL... links the card to a ticket or a page, which opens from the card. Colours are yours to give meaning to. A new story map's legend starts with Yellow for tasks, Cyan for notes, Lime for questions and Rose for edge cases. Change those or add your own in the legend, in the Overview tab, so everyone reads the story map the same way. There's more in Review release progress on a story map. A status shows as a coloured dot on the card. Each slice adds up its points, and shows how much of it is done, in the strip on the left of the slice. Tags cut across the story map, such as backend or design, so you can find related cards in different steps and slices. A card can have as many tags as you like. Select cards by dragging a box around them, starting from an empty part of the story map. A toolbar appears that changes the colour, status or tags of every selected card at once. The large view of a card shows its status, points, tags and link on one line at the bottom. Click Edit there to change them. See Write user stories on a story map.

title: Plan releases with story map slices
description: Group the cards you'll build together into slices, give each one a goal and a date, and link straight to it.

headings.text: Give a slice a goal and a date

text: Slices group the cards you'll build together, such as an MVP and the releases after it. A slice runs across the whole user story map, so you can see what each release covers from start to finish. Make the first slice thin: only the minimum implementation each step needs to work and be useful, so users can get from the first step to the last in the simplest way that works. A first release that does all of one step, and none of the rest, can't be used. Slice an MVP with a story map shows the difference. Everything you can do to a slice is in its menu. Click the ☰ in the strip on the left of the slice, or right-click anywhere in the strip. Copy link to slice copies a link that opens the story map at this slice. Mark Complete folds a finished release into a banner. Click + Slice in the strip to add a new slice straight under that one. Drag a card from one slice to another to move it to a different release. Click a slice's name to open its details. Here you can rename the slice and give it a goal and a target date. The goal and date show behind the ⓘ next to the name, so they're there when you need them without taking up room on the story map. On a phone the details open at the top of the screen, clear of the keyboard. Keep a goal short enough to read at a glance, such as "Order and pay ahead, then pick up". Every slice has its own link. Opening it scrolls the story map to the slice and highlights it for a moment, which is handy in a chat message or a ticket. Renaming the slice never breaks the link, and you can copy it from a locked story map too. Inside a project, the link keeps the project, so the tabs are there when it opens. When a release ships, choose Mark Complete from the slice menu. The slice folds into a banner that shows its goal and how many cards it holds, and its cards stay safe inside. If some cards have a status other than Done, you can move them to the top of the next slice first, or mark the slice complete anyway. Click the banner to see the cards without reopening the slice. They show read-only, and only for you. Choose Reopen to unfold the slice for everyone and edit its cards again. Close folds a slice the same way without marking it complete, for a release you've set aside. Drag a slice by the ↕ handle in its strip to move it up or down the story map. The strip of each slice shows how many of its tasks are done, as a bar and a percentage, and the total story points of its cards. For every slice at once, open the Overview tab. Progress counts the Yellow cards, and any other card with a status. A card in another colour with no status, such as a Cyan note or a Lime question, doesn't count.

title: Reduce duplication with partials
description: Turn steps that repeat across the story map into a partial, use it wherever the journey needs it, and change it in one place.
text: Journeys often share steps. Signing in, paying or checking out can turn up in more than one place, with the same cards under them each time. A partial holds those steps once. Put it wherever the journey needs it, and change it in one place. Click the background of a step, away from its name, to select it. Shift-click another step to select every step in between. Click Create Map Partial in the toolbar that appears, and name the partial. The steps move into the partial, with every card under them in every slice, and a single partial step takes their place. It shows the name of the partial, how many steps it holds, and its first and last step. The Partials tab opens with the new partial in it. Selecting steps needs a mouse, so partials are made on a computer. Once made, they show on every device. Right-click a column and choose Add partial step after, then pick the partial. To swap steps you've already written out for a partial, select them and click the ▾ beside Create Map Partial. Choose Replace with and the name of the partial. The button changes to match, so click it to replace the steps. Replace with swaps the selected steps and their cards for the partial. Ctrl+Z undoes it. Under a partial step, each slice says how many of its cards are inside, such as Show 3 cards. Click it to open the steps of the partial in place, with their cards. Click Hide cards above the steps to fold them back into one. In the Partials tab, Expand and Collapse do the same for one partial, and Expand All for every one. Opening a partial changes the view for you only, not for anyone else on the story map. In the Partials tab, click Edit on the partial. Its steps open on the story map, ready to change like any other: rename them, add cards, or add a step in the space at the end. Rename the partial in the tab too. Click Done when you're finished. Every place the partial is used shows the change. Click Delete in the Partials tab, then choose one: Delete Partial removes the partial, and every partial step that uses it. Restore Columns puts its steps back on the story map as ordinary steps, with their cards. Deleting the last partial step on the story map removes the partial too, after asking first. Ctrl+Z undoes it. Partials reuse steps inside one story map. To keep several whole story maps together, start a project.

title: Review release progress on a story map
description: Read the size of the story map and the progress of each slice in the Overview tab, and give the colours meaning with a legend.
text: The Overview tab at the bottom right sums up the user story map: how big it is, how far each slice has got, and what its colours mean. The top of the tab counts the cards, steps, slices, users, activities and partials on the story map. Each slice has a bar and a count of its tasks that are done, such as 4/8. The bar is coloured by status, so you can see what's in progress or planned as well as what's done. Underneath, the counts add up every status across the story map. Progress counts the Yellow cards, and any other card with a status. A card in another colour with no status, such as a Cyan note or a Lime question, doesn't count. storymaps status shows progress by slice and by status in the terminal. See Check story map progress. The legend says what each colour means, and how many cards use it. A new story map starts with Yellow for tasks, Cyan for notes, Lime for questions and Rose for edge cases. Click a label to rename it. Click a colour to change it. × removes an entry, and + Add adds one. The legend only explains the colours. Removing an entry leaves the cards as they are.

title: Bulk edit story map cards
description: Select many cards or whole columns at once, then move them, change their colour, status or tags, duplicate them or delete them in one go.
text: Select a group of cards and change them all in one go: moves, colour, status, tags, copies or deletes. One action, one undo. Drag a box around the cards, starting from an empty part of the story map. Every card the box touches is selected. Click a card away from its text to select it on its own. Clicking the text edits it instead. Shift+click another card to add it, and Shift+click a selected card to remove it from the selection. Shift+click a step after selecting another step to select every column between them. Click an empty part of the story map, press Esc or click × on the toolbar to clear the selection. Selecting works with a mouse on an unlocked story map. On a phone or tablet, change cards one at a time. The toolbar shows at the bottom of the screen as soon as anything is selected. How many cards and columns are selected. Duplicate and Delete act on the selected cards. Click ▾ beside either to switch it to whole columns. Color, Status and Tags change every selected card at once. Drag any selected card, and the others travel with it. Cards from several columns stay in their own columns and only move up and down, so each task stays under its step. Use this to move a batch of tasks into another slice. A pale card in each column shows where each one will land. Cards from one column can go anywhere, and stack together where you drop them. Ctrl+Z undoes the whole move. Color picks one colour for every selected card. × puts them back to their default colour. Status sets Done, In Progress, Planned or Blocked, or No Status to clear it. Tags lists the tags already on the selection, with × to take one off every card. Below them are the other tags in the story map to add, and a box to type a new one. The colour and status changes show in the progress bars and the Overview tab straight away. Customise story map cards explains what each one is for. Duplicate Cards copies the selected cards into new columns, straight after the selection. Switch to Duplicate Columns to copy whole columns, with their steps and every card under them. Ctrl+D (⌘D on a Mac) duplicates the selected columns too. Delete Cards removes the selected cards, and Delete Columns removes whole columns with every card in them. Both ask first. Delete or Backspace on the keyboard deletes the selected cards, or the columns when steps are selected. Deleted the wrong thing? Ctrl+Z undoes it. Before a big clear-out, make a backup. Select two or more columns and the toolbar offers Create Map Partial. A partial holds a run of steps that more than one journey shares, such as checkout, so you write it once and use it anywhere. Reduce duplication with partials covers how partials work.

title: Build an app from a story map with AI
description: Turn a story map into a working prototype or app with the AI tool you already use, so product teams can build to learn before they commit to a release.

headings.text: Why a story map makes a strong prompt
How the prompt includes the story map

text: A user story map already says who the product is for, what they do and what goes in each release. Build hands all of that to an AI tool as one prompt, and the tool builds it. Pick a slice, pick your tool, copy the prompt and paste it in. Product teams can build to learn. Put a working version of a slice in front of users, see what holds up, and change the story map before the team commits to the release. A request such as "build me a coffee ordering app" leaves the AI to guess who it's for, what they need and what comes first. A story map has settled those questions, and the AI reads it as a structured specification: Users say who it's for. Activities and steps give the journey, in order. Tasks give the features under each step, most important first, with the detail in their bodies. Slices set how much to build, and the goal of a slice says what it's for. Each build takes a few clicks to set up, so a team can try an idea before committing to it. Build a slice as a prototype. Prototype an MVP with AI shows how. Put it in front of users. Add what you learn to the story map as new cards, and move cards between slices if the priorities change. Build again from the updated story map. Keep the story map as the plan, whatever you build. Mark cards done once they're in the real product. Prototype an MVP with AI gets something people can click before anyone writes production code. Build the next release with AI adds a slice to an app you already have. Build one feature with AI tries a single idea from any slice. Prototype a whole product with AI builds every release together. Compare product directions with AI sets different tools or looks side by side. Ask AI about a story map gets answers from an AI tool instead of a build. Click Build at the top right of the story map. On a phone, it's the ⚡ button. Pick the AI tool you'll paste the prompt into. Storymap Slice picks what to build: one slice, or All Slices for the whole story map. Build Mode asks for a Prototype or a Full App. Coding agents can also Add to Existing App. Include map URL puts a link to the story map in the prompt, rather than the whole story map. Add anything else the AI should know in Additional Instructions, such as the look and feel or the audience. Then click Copy Prompt. The line under the prompt says where to paste it. Start with the first slice. It's the smallest version of the product that works from start to finish, so it makes a solid first build. App Builders: Lovable, v0, Replit, Base44 and Bolt. They choose the tech stack for you. AI Chat: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Prototype asks for a single HTML file that opens in a browser, and Full App lets the AI choose the tech and give you the code. AI Coding Agents: Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI give you a command to run in your terminal, so the button reads Copy Command. Cursor, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot get a prompt for the agent chat in your editor. With Include map URL on, the prompt ends with the story map link as .yaml. The prompt stays short, and the AI reads the story map as it is when it opens the link. Turn it off to put the whole story map in the prompt as YAML. ChatGPT and Gemini always get it this way, since they can't open links. For Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI, Use npx storymaps has the command download the story map first, as storymap.yml in the folder you run it in, then start the agent on it. It uses the Storymaps CLI. Turn it off and the agent reads the .yaml link instead.

title: Prototype an MVP with AI
description: Build the first slice of a story map as a clickable prototype with an AI tool, so a product team can learn from users before writing production code.
text: Get something people can click before anyone writes production code. A prototype of the first slice lets a product team build to learn: users try the whole journey, and the team sees what works before committing to the release. Click Build, then choose: Tool: an app builder such as Lovable, or an AI chat. Storymap Slice: MVP. Build Mode: Prototype. Additional Instructions: the look and who it's for, such as "Warm colours and big buttons for phones." Click Copy Prompt and paste it into the tool. In an AI chat, the prototype comes back as a single HTML file that opens in a browser. Put the prototype in front of users, and watch them go through it: Can they get from the first step to the last? Where do they stop or ask for help? What do they expect that isn't there? Add what you learn to the story map as new cards, under the step they relate to, and move cards between slices if the priorities change. With Include map URL on, the same prompt picks up those changes the next time you use it. Paste it in again and compare the new version with the last one.

title: Build the next release with AI
description: Give a coding agent the next slice of a story map, and have it add those features to the app you already have.
text: Already have an app? Run a coding agent in the folder of your project and give it the next slice. Click Build, then choose: Tool: a coding agent, such as Claude Code. Storymap Slice: the next release, such as V1. Build Mode: Add to Existing App. The prompt asks the agent to read the code first, keep what's there working and follow its conventions. Additional Instructions: how you work, such as "Run the existing tests and add tests for each feature." Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI: click Copy Command, and run it in your terminal from the folder of your project. Cursor, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot: click Copy Prompt, and paste it into the agent chat in your editor. The prompt covers every card in the slice, so say if some of it is already built. Mark cards done on the story map once they're in the real product, so the team can see how the release is going.

title: Build one feature with AI
description: Build a single card from any slice of a story map with an AI tool, to try a risky idea before planning it into a release.

headings.text: With a coding agent already running

text: Build one card from any slice. It's a quick way for a product team to try a risky idea from a later release, and learn from it before planning it in. Click Build, then choose: Tool: any of them. Storymap Slice: the slice with the feature in it, such as V2. Build Mode: Prototype to try the idea, or Add to Existing App with a coding agent to put it in your app. Additional Instructions: name the feature, such as "Only build Group ordering." Ask it directly, such as "now build Split payment from the V2 slice."

title: Prototype a whole product with AI
description: Build every release of a story map together as one prototype, to show stakeholders where the product is going.
text: See every release together in one prototype. It's useful for a pitch, or for showing stakeholders where the product is going. Click Build, then choose: Tool: an app builder or an AI chat. Storymap Slice: All Slices. Build Mode: Prototype. Additional Instructions: who will see it, such as "For a pitch to investors. Show each release in order." Ask the people who see it what they'd want first, and what they wouldn't miss. Then move the cards between slices to match.

title: Compare product directions with AI
description: Build the same slice of a story map in different AI tools, or with different instructions, and see which direction works best.
text: A team can build to learn from more than one version. Keep the same user story map behind each build, and change one thing at a time. Set up the slice you want, pick the first tool and click Copy Prompt. Paste it in, then pick the second tool in the Build window and do the same. Each tool gets a prompt set up for it, from the same story map. Keep the slice and the tool the same, and change Additional Instructions for each build: "Warm colours and big buttons for phones." "A clean, minimal look for commuters in a hurry." Show the versions to users, and add what you learn to the story map as new cards.

title: Ask AI about a story map
description: Give an AI tool the link to a story map and ask it what's missing, what looks risky, or to write acceptance criteria and test plans.
text: Build always asks the AI to build something. To ask anything else, give the AI the story map link with .yaml on the end, and your own question: "What's missing from this journey?" "Which tasks in the MVP slice look riskiest?" "Write acceptance criteria for the V1 slice." "Draft a test plan for the MVP slice." ChatGPT and Gemini can't open links, so export the story map as YAML and paste that in. A coding agent such as Claude Code can change the story map too, such as adding the cards you ask for, or marking cards done once they've passed QA. It edits the YAML and pushes it with the Storymaps CLI. See Update a story map with an AI agent.

title: Zoom and pan around a story map
description: Zoom in and out, pan across a big story map, and get back to the whole view in one key press, with a mouse, a keyboard or a touch screen.
text: A user story map opens zoomed to fit the width of the window, so you see the whole journey first. Zoom in to work on part of it, and pan to move around. + zooms in. The percentage shows the zoom. Click it to step through 100%, 75%, 50%, 25% and 10%. − zooms out. Hold Ctrl and scroll, or Cmd on a Mac, to zoom in on the spot under the mouse. The story map zooms from 10% up to 300%. Scroll to move up and down, and hold Shift and scroll to move sideways. Hold the right mouse button and drag to move in any direction. Press the arrow keys to move a little at a time. A right-click that doesn't move still opens the menu for that column. Press Alt+R to zoom the story map back to fit the window. On a Mac, press Shift+0. The story map fits itself again when the window changes size, such as when you go to full screen. Swipe with one finger to move around, and pinch with two to zoom. On a small screen the story map never fits below 50%, so the cards stay readable. Swipe sideways for the rest of the journey. On a tall story map, freeze the top rows so the steps stay in view as you scroll down. Search fades every card that doesn't match, so the ones you want stand out. A link to a slice opens the story map at that slice.

title: Change the story map view
description: Focus mode, full screen, dark mode, other people's cursors and frozen rows, from the view controls at the bottom right.
text: The view controls at the bottom right change how the user story map looks to you. None of them change the story map, or how anyone else sees it. Focus mode hides the status, points, tags and links on cards, for a cleaner story map to present. Full screen fills the screen with the story map. Dark mode switches between light and dark. Cursors shows or hides other people's cursors. Freeze rows keeps the top rows in view as you scroll down. Focus mode leaves just the titles on the cards. The ⤢ still shows when you hover over a card, so you can open one for its detail. Full screen fills your screen with the app, without the browser around it, and zooms the story map to fit. Press Esc twice to leave it, so one press can still close anything that's open, such as search or a card. Some browsers leave full screen on the first press. The story map starts in the same theme as your device. The button switches it, and your browser remembers the choice. On the home page, the switch is in the main menu. When others are on the story map, you see their cursors and names move around. Hide them when they get in the way, such as when presenting. On a tall story map, frozen rows keep the users, activities and steps at the top while you scroll down, so you can always see which step a card is under. You can freeze the users, activities and steps, just the activities and steps, just the steps, or nothing. The choice is saved for your browser only.

title: Search and filter a story map
description: Find cards by their text, or filter the story map by status, colour and tag, without changing it for anyone else.
text: Search fades every card that doesn't match, so the ones you're after stand out where they sit on the user story map. Filters narrow it down by status, colour and tag. Click the magnifying glass at the top, or press Ctrl+F (⌘F on a Mac). Type in Search cards... and the cards that don't match fade as you type. Search reads the text on every card: users, activities, steps and tasks. It ignores capitals, so "pay" finds Pay, Apple Pay / Google Pay and Handle payment failures?. Click the funnel beside the search box to open the filters. Status shows cards with any of the statuses you tick, including No Status. Color shows cards in any of the colours you pick. Tags shows cards with any of the tags you tick. Options that no card uses are greyed out. Set more than one section and a card has to match each of them, such as In Progress and tagged backend. A search and filters work together too. The funnel shows how many filters are on. Clear All turns them off, and Done closes the panel and keeps them. A tag can go on any card, so a tag filter pulls together related work from different steps and slices. On the coffee app story map, tick ai under Tags and click Done. The four AI cards stay bright across V2 and V3, and the rest fade. Tick a second tag to see the cards with either one. To narrow it down, tick something under Status as well, such as Planned. Tags are labels you choose yourself, added to one card or to many at once. They're always saved in lower case. Hover over the card, click … and go to Tags. The tags on the card. Click × to take one off. Type a tag and press Enter, or click one of the tags offered. Select the cards by dragging a box around them or with Shift+click, then click Tags on the toolbar. Bulk edit story map cards has more on selecting cards. The tags at the top are already on the selected cards. A number beside one shows how many have it, when it isn't all of them. Click × to take it off every selected card. Click a tag in the list below to add it to every selected card. To make a new tag, type it in New tag... and press Enter. Tag cards by team or area, such as frontend and backend, and a filter shows one team the work that's theirs across every release. Customise story map cards covers tags. Click × beside the search box, or press Esc. The first Esc closes the filters and the next closes the search. Closing clears the search and every filter, and the story map is back to normal. Search and filters only change what you see. Everyone else on the story map sees it as usual.

title: Share a story map
description: Share a story map with a link, so anyone can open it and work on it with you. No sign-up. Or share it as a picture, or print it.

headings.text: Share a slice or a task
Who can change a shared story map

text: Every user story map has its own link, and anyone with the link can open the story map and work on it with you. Nobody needs to sign up. Share URL copies the link to the story map. Share as image copies a picture of the whole story map, to paste into a chat or a document. Download image saves the picture as a PNG file. When a story map is in a project, the Share menu offers Share project link first. That link opens the project with all its story maps as tabs. Share this map link opens the story map you're on, with the tabs above it. A slice or a task has its own link too, which opens the story map right where it is. Plan releases with story map slices and Add tasks to a story map cover them. Choose Menu → Print. To save a PDF, pick Save as PDF as the printer. Anyone with the link can edit the story map, and everyone sees changes as they happen. To share it without letting people change it, lock it from Menu → Lock Map (Read-only). A locked story map can still be viewed and shared. Keep the lock password somewhere safe, as it can't be recovered.

title: Edit a story map together
description: Work on one story map with the whole team at once, see who's there and where they're pointing, and keep shared notes.
text: Everyone with the link edits the same user story map, at the same time. Changes show for everyone as they happen, with no saving and no refreshing. Copy the link from Share → Share URL and send it to the team. There's no sign-up, so the link is all anyone needs. Share a story map covers the other ways to share. The first time you open a story map on a computer, the app asks for a name for live collaboration. It's optional. Skip it and you show as guest. To change it, click your name at the top right and type a new one. Your name stays in this browser. Others on the story map see it, and it goes in the Log next to your changes. When someone else is on the story map, a count of everyone there shows beside your name. Hover over it to see who they are, with you first. People on a phone show as Mobile user. Several tabs in the same browser count as one person. On a computer, everyone else's pointer moves across the story map with their name on it. When someone drags a card or a column, you see it move with them. Too busy? Click the crossed-out pointer in the controls at the bottom right to hide other pointers. Click it again to bring them back. On a call, point at the card you're talking about. Everyone sees your pointer, so "this one" is enough. Click Notes in the tabs at the bottom right for a notepad that everyone on the story map shares. Type at the same time and each person shows by name where they're typing. Use it for decisions, actions and anything that doesn't belong to one step. The notes save with the story map and go with it when you export it. Keep working. A notice at the bottom of the screen says you're offline, and your changes sync as soon as you reconnect. The app warns you if you try to close the page before they have. Anyone with the link can edit the story map. If you're sharing it publicly, it's wise to lock it and create a backup, in case of unexpected changes.

title: Track changes to a story map
description: See who changed what on a story map in the Log, highlight the cards behind each change, and undo your own changes.
text: The Log tab keeps a running record of the user story map: who's been on it, what they changed and when. Open it after a session to catch up, or while others are editing to see what's changing. Click Log in the tabs at the bottom right of the story map. The summary of the story map. The newest change, at the top. The top of the Log sums up the story map: Created is the date the story map was made. Last edited is how long ago the last change was. Here now counts the people on the story map at this moment. Recent names the people behind the latest changes. Edits counts the changes made to the story map. The Log lists the last 20 changes, newest first. Each one shows the time, who made it and what changed, such as Added card or Changed card status. Changes from earlier days show the date too. Your own changes show as You. Other people show by the name they gave, and changes from a phone show a 📱. Typing is logged once you pause or move on, so a card you rewrite shows as one change, not one per letter. Hover over a change to highlight the cards it touched. Names come from the name each person gives when they open the story map. Edit a story map together covers setting yours. storymaps log shows the same changes in the terminal. Pushes and backups from the CLI show in the Log with a >_. See Read the activity log. ↩ and ↪ at the top step back and forward through your own changes, up to the last 50. Ctrl+Z undoes and Ctrl+Y redoes (⌘Z and ⌘⇧Z on a Mac). The cards that changed flash, so you can see what came back. Undo history lasts until you reload or open another story map. To go back further, or to keep a copy you can return to any time, make a backup.

title: Back up and restore a story map
description: Make a backup of a story map before a big change, restore it in one click, and keep backups when you export and import.
text: A backup is a copy of the whole user story map at one moment. Make one before a big change, and if the change goes wrong, one click puts the story map back. Open Menu → Backups and click Create Backup. Add a note, such as "Before the workshop", so you can tell it apart later. Create Backup makes a new backup. Restore puts the story map back to that backup. Each backup shows its note, the name of the story map, how long ago it was made, its size and how many cards it has. If nothing has changed since one of the backups, no new backup is made, and the app tells you which one matches. A locked story map has to be unlocked before it can be backed up. Click Restore on a backup. The app backs up the story map as it is first, as Auto: before restore, so a restore can be undone too. A locked story map has to be unlocked before it can be restored. The CLI and the app share the same backups. storymaps backup makes one, and storymaps restore puts one back. See Back up and restore from the terminal.
