As well as before a restore, the app backs up the story map before an import, as Auto: before import. The app keeps the 8 newest backups, and the oldest go as new ones come in. Backups are protected from deletion, but can be removed if needed by contacting us. Export a story map as JSON or YAML and its backups go with it. Import the file into another story map and the backups come too, marked as imported so you can tell them apart from the ones it already had. The link to a story map, with .yaml or .json on the end, gives the story map as it is now, without its backups.

title: Start a story map project
description: Keep related story maps together as tabs under one name, with one link that opens them all.

headings.text: Bring in story maps you've opened

text: A project keeps related user story maps together, such as the customer app, the barista screen and the back office of one product. They sit side by side as tabs, one click apart, and one link opens them all. Start a project from any story map. Click Start a project, under the header. On a phone, choose Menu → Start a project. Name the project, such as Coffee shop. Leave it blank and it starts as Untitled project. Click Create project. The story map becomes the first tab, and the address changes to the project link. The app reminds you once to bookmark it. A project never changes the story maps in it. Each story map keeps its own link, and can be in more than one project. The box lists the story maps you've opened recently in this browser. Tick the ones to include, and the button counts them, such as Create project with 3 maps. Only you see this list. Clear list empties it without deleting any story map. Click Add map beside the tabs, then: Tick story maps you've opened recently and click Add maps. Paste the link to a story map and click Add. Click New map to start a blank story map as a new tab. Menu → Copy this map puts the copy in the project too, straight after the original. In a locked project, the copy stays outside it. A project holds up to 20 story maps. Split a bigger product into more than one project. Switch between story maps covers the tabs, Manage a story map project covers renaming and reordering, and Share a story map project gets the whole team on the same link.

title: Switch between story maps
description: Move between the story maps in a project with the tabs, and open one in a new browser tab.

headings.text: If the tabs don't all fit
A story map without the tabs

text: Each user story map in a project is a tab under the header. Click a tab to open that story map. Full screen and your view settings stay as they are, so you keep your place as you switch. Click a tab to open the story map. The open one is underlined. Ctrl-click, or Cmd-click on a Mac, to open it in a new browser tab instead. Use the browser Back button to return to the story map you were on. An arrow shows at each end of the row that has more tabs beyond it. To see them, click an arrow, scroll the mouse wheel over the tabs, or swipe on a phone. When you open a story map, its tab moves into view. A tab shows the name of the story map. Rename the story map at the top and its tab follows as you type. A story map with no name shows as Untitled map. A locked story map shows a padlock after its name. When someone adds, removes or reorders story maps, the tabs update for everyone. Anyone on the same story map sees it straight away, and everyone else within half a minute. The tabs only show at the project link, such as storymaps.io/p/abc12345. The plain link to a story map, such as storymaps.io/abc12345, opens it on its own, even when it's in a project. A project shows in your recent story maps as one entry, with the number of story maps in it. Find your story maps covers the list.

title: Manage a story map project
description: Rename a project, reorder the story maps in it, take one out, or delete the project. The story maps themselves never change.
text: Everything about a project is in the project box. Click the project name, at the left of the tabs, or choose Menu → Manage project. Name renames the project. Project link is the link that opens the project. Copy copies it. Each story map has a row to reorder it or take it out. Delete project deletes the project, and leaves the story maps alone. Lock project protects the project with a password. Lock a story map project covers it. Type a new name in Name, then press Enter or click away to save it. Drag a story map by the handle at the left of its row, or use the up and down arrows. The tabs follow the order of the list. Click Remove and confirm. The story map isn't deleted and still opens at its own link. Remove the last one and the project stays, with no tabs. Its link then offers to start a new story map in it. Click Delete project and confirm. The story maps in it aren't deleted, but the project link stops working. Anyone with the project link can rename, reorder and delete the project unless it's locked, so it's best shared with the people working on the product. Locking a story map doesn't lock the project it's in.

title: Share a story map project
description: Share one link that opens every story map in a project as tabs, or link to one story map in it.

headings.text: Link to one story map in the project
Share a story map on its own

text: Share the project link, and everyone gets every user story map in the project as tabs. No sign-up, and no list of links to keep up to date. Click Share, then Share project link. It copies a link such as storymaps.io/p/abc12345, which opens the project on its first tab. The link is also in the project box, under Project link, with a Copy button. Click Share, then Share this map link. The link opens that story map with the project tabs above it. A slice or task link copied in a project keeps the tabs too. Plan releases with story map slices and Add tasks to a story map cover them. The plain link to a story map, such as storymaps.io/abc12345, never shows the tabs. Use it to share one story map without the rest of the project. Share a story map covers the other ways to share. Anyone with the project link can open every story map in it and change the project unless it's locked, so it's best shared with the people working on the product. The app reminds you once to bookmark a project when you start or rename it. A project you've opened is also in your recent story maps, in the same browser. Find your story maps covers the list.

title: Lock a story map
description: Make a story map read-only with a password, unlock it to edit, change the password or take the lock off.

headings.text: What people can do with a locked story map

text: A lock makes the user story map read-only for everyone without the password. Share the plan wide, and keep the edits to the people who own it. Open Menu → Lock Map (Read-only). Type a password of at least 4 characters. Click Lock Map. Everyone else on the story map goes read-only within seconds, and sees This map is read-only across the top of the screen. You can keep editing in this tab. Keep the password somewhere safe, as it can't be recovered. Anyone with the link can still open it, search it, share it and export it. They can't change cards, slices or notes, import into it, or restore a backup. Open Menu → Unlock Map, type the password and click Unlock. The story map stays unlocked for you until you close the tab. Everyone else still sees it locked. The menu has three more options while you have it unlocked: Re-lock Map locks it again with the same password, in this tab too. Change Password sets a new password. The old one stops working. Remove Lock takes the lock off, so anyone with the link can edit again. The app asks first. Locks, unlocks and removed locks all show in the Log. Lock a story map when it matters to keep it exactly as it is, such as the release the team agreed. It's then the reference everyone works from. Unlock it when it's time to plan again or make updates, and lock it again once they're agreed. storymaps lock locks the story map, and storymaps unlock saves the password on your computer so pushes still work. See Lock and unlock a story map. A locked story map shows a padlock on its tab. To lock every story map in a project at once, lock the project.

title: Lock a story map project
description: Protect the name, tabs and order of a project with a password, and lock its story maps at the same time if you want to.

headings.text: Lock or unlock one story map

text: A locked project keeps its name, user story maps and order as they are for everyone without the password. Use it for a project shared widely, such as a plan other teams follow. Click the project name, at the left of the tabs, and click Lock project. Choose The project, or the option below it, to lock every story map in it too. Type a password of at least 4 characters and click Lock. The project locks straight away, for you too. A story map that already has a lock keeps it, and the project box names any that weren't changed. Keep the password somewhere safe, as it can't be recovered. Nobody can rename or delete the project, or add, remove or reorder its story maps, without the password. Add map shows a padlock. Anyone with the link can still open every story map. A story map can still be edited unless it has its own lock, and a locked story map shows a padlock on its tab. Menu → Copy this map makes a copy outside the project, as nothing can be added to a locked project. Each locked story map has a label in the project box: Project lock means it uses the project password. Map lock means it has a different password. Unlock takes the lock off that story map for everyone, and Lock puts one on using the project password. The row asks for the password when it needs one. To move a story map with a Map lock onto the project password, click Unlock and enter its own password, then click Lock. Click Unlock project in the project box, or click Add map, and type the password. The project stays unlocked for you until you close the tab. Everyone else still sees it locked. The project box then has two more options: Lock again locks it again in this tab. Remove lock takes the lock off for everyone. Tick the box to remove the lock from story maps using the project password too. A story map with a Map lock stays locked.

title: Import a story map
description: Bring a story map in from a JSON, YAML or CSV file, or paste the data straight in.

headings.text: An import replaces the story map
From Jira, Asana, Phabricator or Linear

text: Got a user story map saved as a file? Import it and carry on where you left off. Paste the data or drop the file, and the story map appears in place of the one you're on. Open Menu → Import. Under File, pick JSON, YAML or CSV. Paste the data on the left and click Import JSON, Import YAML or Import CSV. Or drop a file on the right, or click there to pick one. Ctrl+Enter imports pasted data too, or Cmd+Enter on a Mac. Importing swaps everything on the story map for what's in the file, and the app asks before it does. It makes a backup first, as Auto: before import, so you can get the old story map back from Menu → Backups. Undo works too. To keep the story map you're on, start a fresh one with Menu → New and import into that. A locked story map has to be unlocked before you can import into it. JSON is the whole story map, exactly as the app saves it: every card, colour, status, slice, the legend, the notes and the backups. YAML holds the same, laid out to read and write by hand. It's the format to write a story map in a text editor, or to have an AI tool write one for you. CSV lays the story map out as a grid, one column per step, so you can work on it in a spreadsheet. It keeps the cards, slices, legend and notes, but not the backups. The quickest way to see each format is to export a story map you know and open the file. storymaps push sends a YAML or JSON file to the story map, and a file without an id makes a new story map. See Push changes to a story map. Import a JSON or YAML file that holds backups and they're added to the story map, marked as imported so you can tell them apart from the ones it already had. Back up and restore a story map has more. Files are checked before anything changes. If something's wrong, such as a slice that names a step that isn't in the list, the app says what, and the story map stays as it was. The integrations under Menu → Import turn a backlog into a story map. Each has its own page: Jira, Asana, Phabricator and Linear.

title: Export a story map
description: Save a story map as a JSON, YAML or CSV file, or copy the data to paste somewhere else.

headings.text: The story map as it is now
To Jira, Asana, Phabricator or Linear

text: Export saves the user story map as a file you keep. Use it to hold a copy outside the app, move a story map to another site, or work on it in a text editor or a spreadsheet. Open Menu → Export and pick JSON, YAML or CSV under File. The window shows the data, ready to use: Copy to Clipboard copies it, to paste into a message, a ticket or an AI chat. Download File saves it. The file is named after the story map, and you can change the name first. Minify squeezes the JSON onto one line, for when size matters more than reading it. Export works on a locked story map too. JSON is the whole story map, exactly as the app saves it. It's the safest copy to keep. YAML holds the same, laid out to read and edit by hand. CSV lays the story map out as a grid, one column per step, to open in a spreadsheet. All three keep the goal and target date of each slice, and whether it's complete or closed. All three import back in with Menu → Import. Import a story map covers what each one keeps. A JSON or YAML export carries the backups of the story map, so they move with it to another story map or another site. A CSV export doesn't. Back up and restore a story map has more. To get the data without exporting, add .json, .yaml or .csv to the end of the story map link. It always gives the story map as it is right now. Story map data links shows how. storymaps pull saves the story map as YAML, and storymaps convert turns that into JSON. See Pull a story map. For a picture of the story map, or a printed copy, see Share a story map. The integrations under Menu → Export turn the cards into tickets in a tracker. Each has its own page: Jira, Asana, Phabricator and Linear.

title: Story map data links
description: Add .json, .yaml or .csv to the end of a story map link to get the story map as data, always as it is right now.
text: Every user story map link doubles as a data link. Add .json, .yaml or .csv to the end and you get the story map as data instead of the app. No export, no download step, and it's never out of date. Take the link of the story map and add the format to the end: storymaps.io/abc12345.json storymaps.io/abc12345.yaml storymaps.io/abc12345.csv Open one in the browser, or fetch it from a script, such as curl https://storymaps.io/abc12345.yaml. The .csv link downloads as a file, named after the story map, ready to open in a spreadsheet. A story map opened from a project has a longer link, with the project in it. Add the format to the end of that link in the same way: storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345.yaml The story map as it is at that moment, with every change up to then, in the same formats as Export a story map. The JSON and YAML start with the name of the story map, its ID, the site it came from and whether it's locked. Backups aren't included, so whatever reads the link sees only the story map as it is now. To take the backups with you, export to JSON or YAML instead. AI tools. Build with AI points an AI tool at the .yaml link, so it reads the latest story map. Scripts and reports. Fetch the .json or .csv link to pull the story map into anything else you use. A spreadsheet. Open the .csv link for a fresh copy whenever you need one. The links work on a locked story map too. storymaps pull saves the YAML as a file, to edit and push back as a change to the story map. See Pull a story map. A data link has the story map link inside it, so it's best shared where you'd share the story map.

title: User story mapping for Jira
description: Turn a Jira project into a story map, through the Jira API or a CSV export, and send the steps and cards back to Jira as epics and their issues.

headings.text: What you get on the story map

text: Bring a Jira backlog in, lay it out as a journey, then send the plan back. Epics, stories, statuses and story points all come with it, and every card links back to its issue. Jira API fetches the project straight from Jira. Jira CSV reads a CSV file exported from Jira. Choose Menu → Import → Jira → Jira API, or click Jira on the home page. Fill in the Jira Instance URL, such as your-team.atlassian.net, and the Project Key, such as PROJ. Add your Email and an API Token. The Get token link opens the page in Atlassian where you make one. Click Fetch from Jira. Verify Connection checks the details first, if you want to. The API brings in the epics and stories of the project, in rank order. Stories with no epic go in a group called Other. Your credentials aren't stored or logged. They go straight to Jira and are dropped when you're done. In Jira, export the issues as CSV with all fields. The import dialog shows the way: Issues > ... > Export > CSV (all fields). In the story map, choose Menu → Import → Jira → Jira CSV. Drop the file in, or click to pick it. Add your Jira instance URL if you want each card to link back to its issue. Click Continue. The file needs the Summary, Issue key and Issue Type columns. Every issue that isn't an epic comes in under its parent epic. Issues with no parent go in Other (no parent epic). Review Import lists every epic with its stories. Untick anything you don't want, or click Deselect all and tick what you do. The count at the bottom shows what's going in. Importing into an open story map gives you a choice: Add to existing map puts the imported cards to the right of what's there. Replace map swaps the whole story map for the import, and asks first. Either way, a backup is taken before anything changes. Click Import to Map to finish. The cards land in a slice called IMPORTED: Epics & stories, with an empty MVP slice above it and a blank backbone. Epics become lime green cards, tagged epic-01, epic-02 and so on. Stories become cards tagged with their epic, such as epic-01-task, plus their Jira labels. Descriptions go in the body of the card. Statuses become done, in progress or planned. Story points become the points on the card. Links open the issue in Jira. The cards fill up to eight columns from left to right, so an epic and its stories won't share a column. The tags keep them together: search and filter by epic-01 to see one epic at a time. Now make it a story map. Name the users, activities and steps, then drag each card under the step it belongs to. Define the story map backbone shows how. Choose Menu → Export → Jira, then Jira CSV or Jira API. Both work the same way to start: Under Releases, tick the slices to send. Under Status, tick the statuses to send. Each step becomes an epic, named after the step, with its cards under it. Rename an epic, add a description, or untick anything to leave out. A card body becomes the description of its issue. Fill in the Project Name, Project Key and Project Type to import into an existing Jira project, or leave them blank to choose in Jira. Under Status Mapping, match each status to a Jira status. To start with, no status and planned match To Do, in progress matches In Progress, and done matches Done. Each epic can go out as an Epic or a Task. The cards under it go out as tasks. Click Download CSV, then import the file in Jira. The (How to import) link opens the Atlassian guide. Jira doesn't link epics to their issues when it imports a CSV. To keep the links, use the API. Click Step 2: Credentials →. Fill in the Jira Instance URL, Project Key, Email and API Token. Click Export to Jira. Each epic is created with its cards as stories under it, and the progress list links to every issue as it's made. Statuses don't carry over through the API. One export takes up to 200 epics and 2,000 stories.

title: User story mapping for Asana
description: Turn an Asana project into a story map, through the Asana API or a CSV export, and send the steps and cards back to Asana as tasks and subtasks.

headings.text: What you get on the story map

text: Bring an Asana project in, lay it out as a journey, then send the plan back. Sections, tasks, subtasks and what's complete all come with it, and every card links back to its task. Asana API fetches the project straight from Asana. Asana CSV reads a CSV file exported from Asana. Choose Menu → Import → Asana → Asana API, or click Asana on the home page. Paste a Personal Access Token. The Get token link opens the page in Asana where you make one. Paste the Project URL or GID, such as the link to the project list. Click Fetch from Asana. Verify Connection checks the details first, if you want to. The API brings in the sections, tasks and subtasks of the project. Your credentials aren't stored or logged. They go straight to Asana and are dropped when you're done. In Asana, export the project as CSV. The import dialog shows the way: Project > ... > Export/Print > CSV. In the story map, choose Menu → Import → Asana → Asana CSV. Drop the file in, or click to pick it. Click Continue. The file needs a Name column. Subtasks come in under their parent task, matched by name. Review Import lists every group with its tasks. Untick anything you don't want, or click Deselect all and tick what you do. The count at the bottom shows what's going in. When the project has two or more sections, Tag by picks how the tasks group: Group by sections makes each section a group, with its tasks under it. Subtasks aren't imported. Group by tasks & subtasks makes each task a group, with its subtasks under it. Importing into an open story map gives you a choice: Add to existing map puts the imported cards to the right of what's there. Replace map swaps the whole story map for the import, and asks first. Either way, a backup is taken before anything changes. Click Import to Map to finish. The cards land in a slice called IMPORTED: Sections & tasks, or IMPORTED: Epics & stories when grouped by tasks, with an empty MVP slice above it and a blank backbone. Groups become lime green cards, tagged section-01 or epic-01 and so on. Tasks under a group become cards tagged with it, such as section-01-task. Notes go in the body of the card. Complete tasks are marked done, and the rest planned. Links open the task in Asana. The cards fill up to eight columns from left to right, so a group and its tasks won't share a column. The tags keep them together: search and filter by section-01 to see one group at a time. Now make it a story map. Name the users, activities and steps, then drag each card under the step it belongs to. Define the story map backbone shows how. Choose Menu → Export → Asana, then Asana CSV or Asana API. Both work the same way to start: Under Releases, tick the slices to send. Under Status, tick the statuses to send. Each step becomes a parent task, named after the step, with its cards as subtasks. Rename a parent task, or untick anything to leave out. Tick Also create Asana sections for parent tasks? to put each parent task in a section of the same name. A card body becomes the description of its subtask. Click Download CSV, then import the file into your Asana project. The dialog shows the way: click the project name dropdown, then Import, then CSV. Click Step 2: Credentials →. Paste a Personal Access Token and the Project Page URL. Click Export to Asana. The progress list links to every task as it's made. Cards marked done are created complete. One export takes up to 200 parent tasks and 2,000 subtasks.

title: User story mapping for Phabricator
description: Turn Phabricator tasks into a story map, through the Conduit API or a Maniphest CSV export, and send the steps and cards back as parent tasks and subtasks.

headings.text: What you get on the story map

text: Bring Phabricator tasks in, lay them out as a journey, then send the plan back. Parent tasks, subtasks, statuses and points all come with them, and every card links back to its task. Phabricator API fetches the tasks straight from Phabricator. Phabricator CSV reads a CSV file exported from Maniphest. Choose Menu → Import → Phab → Phabricator API, or click Phabricator on the home page. Fill in the Instance URL, such as phabricator.example.com. Paste an API Token. How do I get this? shows where: click your profile picture, go to Settings, then Conduit API Tokens, then Generate Token. Add the Project Tags to import. Use the slug from the /tag/ URL of the project, or type the name with spaces, separated by commas. Click Fetch from Phabricator. Verify Connection checks the details first, if you want to. A task with subtasks becomes a group, with its subtasks under it. Subtasks nested further down come in under the top-level task. Tasks with no parent and no subtasks go in a group called Other. Your API token isn't stored or logged. It goes straight to Phabricator and is dropped when you're done. In Phabricator, export the tasks as CSV. The import dialog shows the way: Maniphest > select tasks > Export as CSV. In the story map, choose Menu → Import → Phab → Phabricator CSV. Drop the file in, or click to pick it. Click Continue. The file needs a Title column. A CSV doesn't say which task is the parent of which, so every task comes in on its own. Review Import lists every task. Untick anything you don't want, or click Deselect all and tick what you do. The count at the bottom shows what's going in. Status, above the list, picks tasks by status: Planned, In Progress and Done. Done tasks are left out to start with. Tick Done to bring them in. Importing into an open story map gives you a choice: Add to existing map puts the imported cards to the right of what's there. Replace map swaps the whole story map for the import, and asks first. Either way, a backup is taken before anything changes. Click Import to Map to finish. The cards land in a slice called IMPORTED: Phabricator tasks, with an empty MVP slice above it and a blank backbone. Parent tasks become lime green cards, tagged epic-01, epic-02 and so on. Subtasks become cards tagged with their parent, such as epic-01-task. Descriptions go in the body of the card. Statuses become planned for open and stalled tasks, in progress for tasks in progress, and done for the rest, such as resolved, declined and invalid. Points become the points on the card. From a CSV, Final Story Points win over Points. Links open the task in Phabricator. The cards fill up to eight columns from left to right, so a parent task and its subtasks won't share a column. The tags keep them together: search and filter by epic-01 to see one parent task at a time. Now make it a story map. Name the users, activities and steps, then drag each card under the step it belongs to. Define the story map backbone shows how. Choose Menu → Export → Phab, then Phabricator API or Phabricator Console API. Both work the same way to start: Under Releases, tick the slices to send. Under Status, tick the statuses to send. Each step becomes a parent task, named after the step, with its cards as subtasks. Rename a parent task, add a description, or untick anything to leave out. Statuses carry over: no status and planned become open, in progress becomes progress, and done becomes resolved. A card body becomes the description of its task. Click Step 2: Credentials →. Fill in the Instance URL and API Token, and add Project Tags so the tasks land in the right projects. Click Export to Phabricator. The progress list links to every task as it's made. One export takes up to 200 parent tasks and 2,000 subtasks. The console export runs in your own browser, on your Phabricator site, so your API token never reaches Storymaps.io. Click Step 2: Import →. Fill in the Instance URL and API Token, and add Project Tags. Open your Phabricator site, open the browser console, then paste the first piece of code and press Enter. Copy copies it. Paste the second piece of code in the same console and press Enter to create the tasks.

title: User story mapping for Linear
description: Turn a Linear team into a story map, through the Linear API or a CSV export, and send the steps and cards back to Linear as parent issues and sub-issues.

headings.text: What you get on the story map

text: Bring a Linear backlog in, lay it out as a journey, then send the plan back. Projects, parent issues, statuses, estimates and labels all come with it. Linear API fetches the issues of a team straight from Linear. Linear CSV reads a CSV file exported from Linear. Choose Menu → Import → Linear → Linear API, or click Linear on the home page. Paste an API Key. The Create key link opens the page in Linear where you make one. Fill in the Team Key, the letters before the number in an issue ID: JAC from JAC-5. Click Fetch from Linear. Verify Connection checks the details first, if you want to. Your credentials aren't stored or logged. They go straight to Linear and are dropped when you're done. In Linear, export your issues as CSV. The import dialog shows the way: Settings > Export > Export CSV. In the story map, choose Menu → Import → Linear → Linear CSV. Drop the file in, or click to pick it. Click Continue. The file needs a Title column. Issues from a CSV don't link back to Linear. Review Import lists every group with its issues. Untick anything you don't want, or click Deselect all and tick what you do. The count at the bottom shows what's going in. Tag by picks how the issues group: Group by projects makes each project a group, with its issues under it. Issues with no project go in Other (no project). Parent issues aren't imported. Group by parent issues makes each parent issue a group, with its sub-issues under it. Issues with no parent go in Other (no parent issue). It starts on projects when there are two or more, and on parent issues otherwise. Importing into an open story map gives you a choice: Add to existing map puts the imported cards to the right of what's there. Replace map swaps the whole story map for the import, and asks first. Either way, a backup is taken before anything changes. Click Import to Map to finish. The cards land in a slice called IMPORTED: Projects & issues, or IMPORTED: Parent issues & sub-issues, with an empty MVP slice above it and a blank backbone. Groups become lime green cards, tagged project-01 or parent-01 and so on. Issues under a group become cards tagged with it, such as project-01-task, plus their Linear labels. Descriptions go in the body of the card. Statuses become done, in progress or planned. Estimates become the points on the card. Links open the issue or project in Linear. The cards fill up to eight columns from left to right, so a group and its issues won't share a column. The tags keep them together: search and filter by project-01 to see one group at a time. Now make it a story map. Name the users, activities and steps, then drag each card under the step it belongs to. Define the story map backbone shows how. Linear export goes through the API. Choose Menu → Export → Linear → Linear API: Under Releases, tick the slices to send. Under Status, tick the statuses to send. Each step becomes a parent issue, named after the step, with its cards as sub-issues. Rename a parent issue, add a description, or untick anything to leave out. Click Step 2: Credentials →. Paste an API Key and fill in the Team Key. Click Export to Linear. A card body becomes the description of its sub-issue, and card points become its estimate. Statuses don't carry over. The progress list links to every issue as it's made. One export takes up to 200 parent issues and 2,000 sub-issues.

title: Install the Storymaps CLI
description: Install the Storymaps CLI with npm, or run it with npx without installing, to pull, edit and push story maps from the terminal.
text: The Storymaps CLI pulls a user story map into a YAML file, and pushes your changes back. It needs Node.js 18 or later. npm install -g storymaps Check it's there. It prints the version number. storymaps --version npx downloads the CLI and runs it in one go. It's how Build with AI in the app starts a coding agent. npx storymaps pull storymaps.io/abc12345 The CLI is open source on GitHub. Clone it and link it, so the storymaps command runs your copy. git clone https://github.com/jackgleeson/storymaps-cli.git cd storymaps-cli npm install npm link storymaps --help lists every command, and storymaps <command> --help shows what one command takes. The Command reference has the same on one page.

title: Create a story map from the terminal
description: Run storymaps init to make a new story map as a storymap.yml file, registered on the server and ready to edit, push and open in the browser.
text: storymaps init makes a new user story map: a storymap.yml file in the folder you're in, and the story map it belongs to on the server. storymaps init The CLI prints the new file too. It's a starter story map, with one of each kind of card to type over: From here, edit the YAML and push it, or open it in the browser and carry on there. If the folder already has a storymap.yml, the CLI asks before it overwrites it. With no connection, the file is still made, and the CLI says so: storymaps init The first push makes the story map on the server, adds its id to the file, and prints its link: storymaps push Any story map file without an id works the same way, such as one written by hand or by an AI agent. --site makes the story map on another Storymaps.io server, such as one your company runs. See Use the CLI with your own server. storymaps init --site storymaps.yourcompany.com

title: Open a story map in the browser
description: Run storymaps open to see the story map in storymap.yml, or any story map by its link, in your browser.

headings.text: The story map in your file

text: storymaps open opens the user story map in your browser, and prints its link. In a folder with a storymap.yml, it opens the story map the file came from: storymaps open The file needs an id. A new file made offline gets one on its first push. Give it a link or an ID: storymaps open storymaps.io/abc12345 A link to a story map in a project works too, such as storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345. It opens the story map on its own, without the project tabs.

title: Pull a story map
description: Run storymaps pull to download a story map as storymap.yml, then pull again to bring in changes made in the browser.
text: storymaps pull downloads a user story map as storymap.yml, in the folder you're in, to edit and push back. Give it the link of the story map: storymaps pull [target] [-f <path>] [--force] storymaps pull storymaps.io/abc12345 The link can be a whole address, such as https://storymaps.io/abc12345, or the ID on its own. A link to a project, or to a story map in one, such as storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345, pulls into a storymaps folder instead. See Pull a project. Changes made in the browser don't reach the file by themselves. Run storymaps pull with no link to bring them in. The file knows which story map it came from. storymaps pull It lists what changed, and asks before it overwrites the file. --force skips the question. If nothing changed, it says Already up to date. Pull replaces the whole file, edits and all. Push or copy your own changes first. -f pulls into a different file, so one folder can hold several story maps: storymaps pull storymaps.io/k3x9w2pq -f checkout.yml Most other commands take -f too, such as storymaps push -f checkout.yml. diff takes the file name on its own: storymaps diff checkout.yml.

title: Edit the story map YAML
description: How storymap.yml lays out a story map, the fields a card and a slice take, and how to add and change cards before you push.
text: Every user story map has structured data behind it, and storymap.yml is its source code. The file reads top to bottom the way the story map reads: the steps from left to right, then each slice with its cards under their step. Edit it in any text editor. Part of the Coffee App, as it comes from a pull: The story map. Its name, its ID and the site it's on. Leave id and site as they are, so the push goes back to the same story map. Users and activities, the cards above the steps. Each one names the step it sits over. Steps, from left to right. Slices, from top to bottom. Each slice lists its cards under the name of their step. A card. Only name is needed. In the Coffee App, mark Choose size done, and add a card to the V1 slice. The green lines are the new ones: Keep the spaces at the start of each line as they are. YAML uses them to tell what belongs to what. Then see what changed, and push it. name The title on the card. body The text inside the card, on one line or several. status done, in-progress, planned or blocked. points Story points, as a number. Each slice adds them up. tags A list, such as [payments, mobile]. color The card colour, as a hex code, such as "#fef08a". url A link, such as a ticket in a tracker. name The name of the slice, such as MVP. goal What the slice is for, in up to 200 characters. targetDate The date it's aimed at, as "2026-11-24". collapsed true when the slice is folded away as finished. closedReason Why it's finished: complete or closed. stories The cards, under the name of their step. legend lists the colours of the legend, each with its label. notes holds the text of the Notes tab. A step called spacer is an empty column, for space between groups of steps. locked says whether the story map is locked. Change that with storymaps lock. Validate the file to check it before a push. A push checks it too, and stops before changing anything if it's not right.

title: See what changed in a story map
description: Run storymaps diff to compare storymap.yml with the story map on the server, slice by slice or line by line, before you push.
text: storymaps diff compares your file with the user story map on the server, so you can check a change before you push it. storymaps diff [source] [target] [--full] After the change in Edit the story map YAML: storymaps diff Each line is a slice and what changed in it: + for cards added, - for cards removed and ~ for cards changed, with the fields that changed. If the file matches the story map, it says No differences. --full shows the lines that changed, with a few lines either side. The two columns of numbers are the line numbers on the server and in your file. storymaps diff --full Give it two files to compare them with each other, without the server: storymaps diff storymap.yml before-the-workshop.yml With one file, it compares that file with its story map: storymaps diff checkout.yml. Give it a link or an ID to compare your file of that story map with the server, wherever the file is: storymaps diff storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345 In a project folder, it compares every story map, and lists the ones that differ: storymaps diff --full shows the lines that changed in each one. See Push changes to a project.

title: Push changes to a story map
description: Run storymaps push to send the changes in storymap.yml back to the story map, and what happens when the story map changed in the browser or is locked.

headings.text: If it changed in the browser

text: storymaps push sends the changes in your file back to the user story map. They show in the browser, and in the activity log with the CLI icon. storymaps push [target] [-f <path>] [--force] See what changed since the last pull. storymaps diff Push it. The CLI lists the changes again as it goes. storymaps push Steps, slices and cards that still match keep their IDs, so links to them keep working. When someone changed the story map after your last pull, the push stops, and nothing changes on the server: storymaps push The list shows what your push would do to the story map as it is now. Here, - V2: 1 card is a card someone added in the browser, which your file doesn't have. To keep both: Copy your file, such as to mine.yml. Run storymaps pull, which brings in the changes from the browser. Make your changes again. storymaps diff storymap.yml mine.yml shows what they were. Push. --force pushes anyway, and replaces what changed in the browser. Use it only when your file should win. The CLI asks for the password, then pushes: storymaps push After storymaps unlock, it uses the saved password without asking. A script can give it in STORYMAPS_PASSWORD. See Use the CLI in scripts and CI. For every story map in a project at once, see Push changes to a project. A file without an id makes a new story map on the first push. See Create a story map from the terminal.

title: Pull a project
description: Run storymaps pull with a project link to download every story map in the project into one storymaps folder, then pull again to bring in changes made in the app.

headings.text: A story map taken out of the project
A link to one story map in the project
Next to a single story map

text: storymaps pull with a project link downloads every user story map in the project into one storymaps folder, a file for each. Give it the link of the project: storymaps pull [project link] [--dir <folder>] [--force] [--yes] storymaps pull storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq Each file is named by the ID of its story map, so renaming a story map in the app never puts a file out of step. The story map name is on the first line of each file. The folder keeps a repo tidy: one new folder, however many story maps the project has. Pull it somewhere else with --dir, such as --dir plans. Each file says which project it's in, straight after its id: It's written only when the story map is fetched through its project. A plain link to the same story map leaves it out. Push ignores it, apart from adding a new story map to the project. Run storymaps pull with no link, from the folder that holds storymaps, or from inside it. Story maps added in the app get new files, and changes are listed before anything is overwritten: storymaps pull One question covers every file. --force skips it. A story map removed from the project in the app keeps its file. Pull takes the project line out, so a later push can't put it back by accident: storymaps pull The CLI never moves, renames or deletes a file, so a story map open in an editor never looks deleted. Delete the file yourself when you no longer need it. The address bar in the app always shows a story map inside its project, such as storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345. Pulled with that link, the CLI asks whether you meant the story map or the whole project: storymaps pull storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345 It only asks the first time. Once the folder holds the project, a link to one of its story maps pulls just that one. Run with no terminal, such as from a script, it takes just the story map and says how to pull the rest: storymaps pull storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq/abc12345 --yes does the same in a terminal, without asking. A project in reach wins: storymaps below you, or project files in the folder you're in. A storymap.yml in the same folder is one -f storymap.yml away, and every command starts by saying so: Using the project in storymaps/. Add -f storymap.yml for the map in storymap.yml. A folder with only storymap.yml works as it always has. To bring that story map into the project, see Start a project from the terminal. Next: Push changes to a project.

title: Push changes to a project
description: Run storymaps push in a project folder to check every story map, then push only the ones that changed. Nothing is sent if any check fails.

headings.text: Nothing is sent until everything checks out
A fresh copy of the repo

text: storymaps push in a project folder checks every user story map, then pushes only the ones that changed. storymaps diff shows what a push would change, story map by story map: storymaps diff Then push: storymaps push Run both from the folder that holds storymaps, or from inside it. Push checks every file, every conflict and every password before it sends anything. If one story map fails a check, none are pushed, so a project never ends up half pushed. If a story map changed in the app since you last pulled: storymaps push Pull shows both sets of changes and asks before it overwrites your file: storymaps pull That replaces your edits to that story map, so make them again, then push. --force does the opposite, replacing the changes made in the app. The CLI remembers what it last pulled on each computer. A file it has never pulled, such as one from a fresh clone of a repo, can't show whether its story map changed on the server since, so push stops: storymaps push Story maps locked with the project password need it once, for all of them. After storymaps project unlock --maps, it isn't asked for at all. A story map with its own password asks for that one separately. Run with no terminal, such as by an agent or a script, push can't ask, so it stops and says how to give the password: storymaps push See Use the CLI in scripts and CI for STORYMAPS_PASSWORD. A file whose story map isn't in the project, such as one removed in the app, is skipped, and push says how to add it back with storymaps project add. A file whose story map is no longer on the server, because it was deleted, is skipped too. A deleted story map never comes back at its old link. A file without an id stops push, as it isn't on the server yet. Add it with storymaps project add. YAML files without a project line, such as a docker-compose.yml, aren't story maps in the project, and push never looks at them. To push one story map on its own, name its file: storymaps push -f storymaps/m7q2r8tz.yml.

title: Start a project from the terminal
description: Run storymaps project init to start a project of story maps, and storymaps project add to add a new story map, a file, or a story map that already exists.

headings.text: Add a story map you already have

text: storymaps project init starts a project, and storymaps project add adds user story maps to one. Both write the story maps into the storymaps folder. Give it a name, and the story map files to start from: storymaps project init [--name <name>] [files...] [--dir <folder>] storymaps project init --name "Bakery" ordering.yml rewards.yml Each file becomes a story map in the project. The files you started from are left as they are, so delete them once you've checked the new ones. With no files, the project starts with one new story map, My Story Map. With no --name, it's called Untitled project, as in the app. Rename either in the app. storymaps project add [file or link] [--name <name>] [--project <link>] storymaps project add --name "Merch" It says the lock the story map has, so you know whether to lock it too. Adding to a locked project asks for the project password. Give it the file. A story map that's already on the server keeps its ID, its link and its activity log, and joins the project: storymaps project add storymap.yml A file that isn't on the server yet, such as one you wrote yourself, becomes a new story map with its content. A story map you haven't pulled can be added by its link instead: storymaps project add storymaps.io/n5b8d2wq. With no connection, the CLI makes the ID itself, so the file is still named by ID: storymaps project add --name "Breakfast" The next push creates it: storymaps push If another story map already has that ID, which is very rare, push gives the new one a fresh ID and renames its file to match. That's the one time the CLI renames a file. project add adds to the project in the storymaps folder, or in the folder you're in. With no project folder yet, such as on a new computer, name the project with --project storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq. Renaming a project, and reordering, removing and deleting its story maps, stay in the app. See Manage a story map project.

title: Lock and unlock a project
description: Run storymaps project lock to lock a project, and its story maps if you want, and storymaps project unlock to push to it or take the lock off.

headings.text: See which story maps are locked

text: storymaps project lock locks the project, with the same two choices as Lock project in the app. See Lock a story map project for what a locked project does. Choose what the password locks, then type a password of at least 4 characters, twice: storymaps project lock The project keeps its name, story maps and order as they are. What's on each story map can still be edited. The project and its maps also locks every story map that isn't locked yet. A story map with its own password keeps it. --maps picks the second choice without asking, and --yes the first. A story map added after the project was locked isn't locked. --maps on a locked project asks for its password and locks only the story maps that aren't locked yet: storymaps project lock --maps storymaps status ends each line with the lock that story map has: storymaps status locked means locked with the project password, and own lock means a story map with its own password. storymaps project unlock checks the password and saves it on this computer, as typing it in the app does. Then it asks whether to unlock the story maps that use the project password too, so pushes and backups don't ask for it: storymaps project unlock --maps answers yes without asking. Everyone else still sees the project and its story maps locked. --remove takes the lock off for everyone, after a warning. It asks whether to take the lock off the story maps that use the project password too. The answer is no unless you say yes, as in the app: storymaps project unlock --remove --remove --maps takes them all off without asking. storymaps lock and storymaps unlock work on one story map, named with -f. In a project folder without it, they say so: storymaps lock See Lock and unlock a story map.

title: Check story map progress
description: Run storymaps status for progress across the story map and in each slice, counts by status, and the cards that are blocked.

headings.text: The story map in your file
Any story map, without a file

text: storymaps status shows how far the user story map has got: overall, slice by slice, and by status. After the push in Push changes to a story map: storymaps status Overall Progress counts the cards marked done against all the cards. Slices does the same for each slice, with its points when cards have them. Status counts the cards with each status. Blocked shows only when a card is blocked, and lists each one by name. Cards in a legend colour whose label doesn't say task, such as Notes or Questions, are left out of the counts. Give it a link to check a story map you haven't pulled: storymaps status storymaps.io/abc12345 It reads the story map as it is on the server, so it's up to date with changes made in the browser. Without a link, it reads your file, which may not be. In a project folder, it shows a line for each story map, in the order of the tabs, and a total: storymaps status When the project or its story maps are locked, each line ends with its lock. See Lock and unlock a project. Give it a project link, such as storymaps status storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq, to check a project you haven't pulled.

title: Read the activity log
description: Run storymaps log to see the recent changes to a story map in the terminal, newest first, with who made them and where.
text: storymaps log shows the recent changes to the user story map, newest first. It's the same log as the activity log in the app. storymaps log Each line has the time, where the change came from and what it was: >_ is the CLI, such as a push or a backup. 🌐 is the browser, with the name of the person. 📱 is a phone or tablet. Changes from today show the time. Older ones show the date too. Give it a link to read the log of a story map you haven't pulled: storymaps log storymaps.io/abc12345

title: Lock and unlock a story map
description: Run storymaps lock to make a story map read-only with a password, storymaps unlock to push to it, and storymaps unlock --remove to take the lock off.
text: A lock makes the user story map read-only for everyone without the password. It's the same lock as Lock Map in the app. See Lock a story map for what people can still do with a locked one. Type a password of at least 4 characters, then type it again: storymaps lock Keep the password somewhere safe, as it can't be recovered. storymaps unlock checks the password and saves it on this computer, so push, backup and restore work without asking for it. The story map stays locked for everyone else. storymaps unlock Without it, a push to a locked story map asks for the password each time. --remove takes the lock off for everyone, so anyone with the link can edit again: storymaps unlock --remove Give it a link to lock or unlock a story map you haven't pulled, such as storymaps lock storymaps.io/abc12345. A script can't type a password, so give it in STORYMAPS_PASSWORD. For storymaps lock, it's the new password: STORYMAPS_PASSWORD="$MAP_PASSWORD" storymaps lock See Use the CLI in scripts and CI. In a project folder, name the story map with -f, such as storymaps lock -f storymaps/m7q2r8tz.yml. Afterwards the CLI says which lock the story map has: the project password, if that's what you typed, or its own. To lock the whole project, see Lock and unlock a project.

title: Back up and restore from the terminal
description: Run storymaps backup before a big change, storymaps backups to list them, and storymaps restore to put the story map back. The app shows the same backups.
text: A backup is a copy of the whole user story map at one moment, kept on the server. The CLI and the app share the same backups, so one made in the terminal shows in Menu → Backups in the app, and the other way round. Add a note with -m, so you can tell it apart later: storymaps backup -m "Before the planning session" If nothing has changed since one of the backups, no new one is made, and the CLI says which one matches: storymaps backup Newest first, each with the ID to restore it by: storymaps backups Give it the backup ID. It shows the backup and asks first. --force skips the question. storymaps restore 6e3cb08697e7 It backs up first. The story map as it was before the restore becomes a backup too, so a restore can be undone with another restore. It changes the story map, not your file. Run storymaps pull afterwards. Until you do, a push stops with a conflict, so an old file can't undo the restore by accident. The server keeps the 8 newest backups of each story map, and the oldest go as new ones come in. Backups are protected from deletion, but can be removed if needed by contacting us. A locked story map needs its password to back up or restore. The CLI uses the one saved by storymaps unlock, or asks for it. In a project folder, storymaps backup backs up every story map with the same note, such as before an agent makes a big change: storymaps backup -m "Before the release" A story map that hasn't changed since its last backup reuses it, so it doesn't use up one of its 8. A project password is asked for once. storymaps backups lists the newest backup of each story map: storymaps backups Restoring still puts back one story map at a time. The backup ID says which, so there's no need to name the file: storymaps restore ca95776ac648 For backups in the app, see Back up and restore a story map.

title: Validate and convert story map files
description: Run storymaps validate to check a story map file before a push, and storymaps convert to turn YAML into JSON and back.
text: Both work on files only, without the server. storymaps validate storymap.yml When something's wrong, it lists what, and nothing else happens: storymaps validate storymap.yml It checks that there are steps, that step names aren't used twice, and that every card, user and activity sits under a step that exists. A status that isn't done, in-progress, planned or blocked is a warning, which doesn't stop a push. It reads JSON files too, such as one exported from the app. Push runs the same checks before it sends anything. Give it a folder to check every story map file in it, such as a project: storymaps validate storymaps It also checks that a project line holds a project ID. storymaps convert storymap.yml --to json --out storymap.json storymaps convert export.json --out storymap.yml YAML is the default, so --to yaml can be left out. Without --out, the result prints in the terminal instead, ready to pipe into another command. The app imports both, so a converted file can go straight in. See Import a story map.

title: Hand a story map to an AI coding agent
description: Pull a story map into storymap.yml and start Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI on it, as a specification to build from, one slice at a time.

headings.text: Let the app write the command
Steer it a slice at a time

text: A story map makes a good specification for an AI coding agent. storymap.yml lists every step of the journey and the cards under each one, slice by slice, so the agent can build a slice and know what comes later. In the app, click Build and pick Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, with Use npx storymaps ticked. Copy Command gives a command that pulls the story map, then starts the agent on it: npx storymaps pull --force https://storymaps.io/abc12345 && claude "The storymap file @storymap.yml describes a product plan in user story map format. Use it as a structured specification. Your task: build a functional prototype of the features listed in the 'MVP' slice." Run it in the folder the app should go in. See Build an app from a story map with AI for the choices in Build. Pull the story map, then start the agent with your own words: storymaps pull storymaps.io/abc12345 claude "Read storymap.yml. Build the MVP slice as a web app." For a project of several story maps, pull the project, so the agent gets every story map as one specification: storymaps pull storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq claude "The story maps in storymaps/ describe one product. Read them all, then build the MVP slice of Coffee App." Have the agent pass --yes to the CLI, so it never waits on a question. See Pull a project. Once the agent is running, ask for more in the same session: "Now build search from the V1 slice." "Add Group ordering from V2, and nothing else from that slice." "Which cards in the MVP slice aren't built yet?" storymap.yml is a copy of the story map at the moment it was pulled. When the plan changes in the browser, run storymaps pull before the next round, so the agent works from the story map as it is now. To have the agent change the story map too, see Update a story map with an AI agent.

title: Update a story map with an AI agent
description: Ask an AI coding agent to add cards, tag them or mark them done, and it edits storymap.yml and pushes the change with the Storymaps CLI.
text: A coding agent that can run commands, such as Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, can change the user story map as well as read it. It edits storymap.yml, checks the change with storymaps diff, and sends it with storymaps push, the same as you would. Say what to change and where, in plain words: "Add cards to the V1 slice for loyalty points, under Pay." "Tag every card under Pay with payments." "Split Group ordering into smaller cards in the same slice." "Group ordering passed QA in the real app. Mark its card done." Then ask it to show the diff and push. The commands it runs look like this: storymaps pull storymaps backup -m "Before the loyalty cards" storymaps diff storymaps push The change shows in the browser straight away, and in the activity log with the CLI icon. Pull first. The story map may have changed in the browser since the agent last pulled. Back up first. If the change goes wrong, restore the backup, from the terminal or the app. Read the diff. Ask the agent to stop after storymaps diff, and push once you've seen it. Mark done only what's done. Done on the story map means done in the real product. Cards for a prototype the agent built to learn from stay as they are. If a push stops with a conflict, ask the agent to copy the file, pull, and make its changes again. See Push changes to a story map. The agent can't type a password. Run storymaps unlock yourself first, and its pushes use the saved password. For a locked project, run storymaps project unlock --maps, which does the same for every story map that uses the project password. The agent never sees the password either way. Without it, a push stops before it sends anything and says what to do. In CI, give the password in STORYMAPS_PASSWORD instead. See Use the CLI in scripts and CI. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini in the browser can't run the CLI. Ask one to write the cards as YAML in the shape of storymap.yml, add them to the file yourself, then push. See Edit the story map YAML for the shape.

title: Use the CLI with your own server
description: Point the Storymaps CLI at your own Storymaps.io server with a link, --site or the site line in storymap.yml.

headings.text: Name the server in the link

text: The CLI works with any Storymaps.io server, such as one your company runs. It goes to storymaps.io unless it's told otherwise. Every command that takes a link takes one on your server: storymaps pull storymaps.yourcompany.com/abc12345 The pulled file says where it came from, in its site line, so pull, push and the rest go back to the same server without the link: --site makes the new story map on your server: storymaps init --site storymaps.yourcompany.com A server on your own computer always names its port, such as localhost:3000. It's reached over http: storymaps init --site localhost:3000 The file then says site: localhost:3000, so every command finds the server. localhost on its own stops with a message asking for the port, so a command never goes to a port you didn't choose. Give the whole address, such as --site http://192.168.0.20:8080 or --site https://localhost:8443. The file names it in full, so every command after it uses the same address. Each request from the CLI names it and its version, such as storymaps-cli/1.4.2, so the server logs can tell the CLI apart from other scripts.

title: Use the CLI in scripts and CI
description: How the Storymaps CLI answers its own questions with no terminal, the --yes and --force options, and STORYMAPS_PASSWORD for locked story maps in scripts and CI.
text: The CLI only asks a question in a terminal. Run from a script, CI or most AI agent tools, there's no terminal, and every question has an answer you can give up front. How much to do, such as one story map or the whole project Takes the usual answer, and says so --yes Before overwriting or removing something, such as Apply changes? Stops, and says to use --force --force A password Stops, and says how to give one See below --yes never stands in for --force, so it can't overwrite anything by accident. Some agent tools do run commands in a terminal, so have agents pass --yes every time. A pull with changes to apply and no terminal: storymaps pull Passwords are never options, as options end up in shell history and agent logs. They come from one of three places: Typed in a terminal. Remembered on this computer after storymaps unlock or storymaps project unlock --maps. Unlock once yourself, and an agent can push without ever seeing the password. STORYMAPS_PASSWORD, an environment variable, for scripts and CI. Set it from the secrets of the pipeline. With none of them, a command stops before it changes anything: storymaps push With the variable set: STORYMAPS_PASSWORD="$MAP_PASSWORD" storymaps push It works with every command that needs a password. For storymaps lock, it's the new password, so nothing is asked: STORYMAPS_PASSWORD="$MAP_PASSWORD" storymaps lock Across a whole project, the variable is only tried on the project and the story maps locked with its password. A story map with its own password is never sent the wrong one, which would count against the limit on wrong passwords. A pipeline can lock a project, and its story maps, once a release is agreed: STORYMAPS_PASSWORD="$RELEASE_PASSWORD" storymaps project lock --maps See Lock and unlock a project.

title: Command reference
description: Every Storymaps CLI command and option, from init, pull, diff and push to status, log, locks, backups, validate, convert and the project commands.

headings.text: One story map or a whole project

text: Every command and option. A target is a user story map: an ID, a link such as storymaps.io/abc12345, or a whole address. A link to a story map in a project works too. Left out, the command uses the story map in storymap.yml, or every story map in the project folder. storymaps --help lists the commands, storymaps <command> --help shows one, and storymaps --version prints the version. storymaps init Make a new story map and its storymap.yml storymaps open Open the story map in the browser storymaps pull Download a story map, or a whole project storymaps push Send your changes to the story map storymaps diff See what changed before you push storymaps status Show progress by slice and by status storymaps log Show the activity log storymaps lock Lock a story map with a password storymaps unlock Save the password on this computer, or take the lock off storymaps backup Back up a story map, or every story map in a project storymaps backups List the backups of a story map storymaps restore Put a story map back to a backup storymaps validate Check a story map file without the server storymaps convert Turn YAML into JSON, or JSON into YAML storymaps project init Start a project storymaps project add Add a story map to the project storymaps project lock Lock the project, or the project and its story maps storymaps project unlock Unlock the project on this computer, or take its lock off storymaps <command> works on story maps: one, named with -f or a link, or every story map in the project folder. storymaps project <command> changes the project itself. With no -f or link, a project in reach wins: the folder named with --dir, a storymaps folder below you, or project files in the folder you're in. With no project in reach, storymap.yml means one story map. See Pull a project. Questions are only asked in a terminal. -y, --yes takes the usual answer, and --force answers the questions that guard against overwriting or removing something. Passwords are typed, remembered after an unlock, or taken from STORYMAPS_PASSWORD. See Use the CLI in scripts and CI. Makes a new storymap.yml in the folder you're in, and the story map on the server. Never joins a project. See Create a story map from the terminal. storymaps init [-s <site>] -s, --site <site> The server to make it on, such as storymaps.yourcompany.com, localhost:3000 or http://192.168.0.20:8080. A server on your computer names its port. storymaps.io if left out. storymaps init storymaps init -s storymaps.yourcompany.com Opens the story map in the browser, and prints its link. In a project folder, opens the project at its first story map. See Open a story map in the browser. storymaps open [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. storymaps open storymaps open -f storymaps/abc12345.yml Downloads the story map as YAML, or every story map in a project. Shows what changed and asks before it overwrites a file. See Pull a story map and Pull a project. storymaps pull [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] [--force] [--yes] target A story map, or a project link such as storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq. -f, --file <path> The file to write, for one story map. storymap.yml if left out. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --force Overwrite files without asking. -y, --yes Take the usual answers, such as just the story map for a link to one in a project. storymaps pull storymaps.io/abc12345 storymaps pull storymaps.io/p/k8f2m9xq storymaps pull --force Sends the file to the story map, or every changed story map in a project. Stops if a story map changed since the last pull, and in a project checks everything before sending anything. See Push changes to a story map and Push changes to a project. storymaps push [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] [--force] -f, --file <path> The file to push, YAML or JSON, for one story map. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --force Skip the conflict check, and replace what changed on the server. storymaps push storymaps push -f plans/checkout.yml storymaps push --force Compares a file with its story map, or with another file, or every story map in a project with the server. See See what changed in a story map. storymaps diff [source] [target] [--full] [--dir <folder>] source The file to compare, or a link or ID to compare your file of that story map. storymap.yml if left out, or the whole project in a project folder. target A second file. Left out, it compares with the story map on the server. --full Show the changed lines, not only a summary. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. storymaps diff storymaps diff --full storymaps diff before.yml after.yml Shows progress overall, by slice and by status, and the cards that are blocked. In a project, a line for each story map with its lock, and a total. See Check story map progress. storymaps status [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] target A story map or a project on the server, or a file. -f, --file <path> The file to read, for one story map. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. storymaps status storymaps status storymaps.io/abc12345 Shows the activity log of one story map, newest first. See Read the activity log. storymaps log [target] [-f <path>] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from. storymap.yml if left out. storymaps log storymaps log storymaps.io/abc12345 Locks one story map with a password of at least 4 characters, asked for twice. See Lock and unlock a story map. storymaps lock [target] [-f <path>] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from. Needed in a project folder. storymaps lock Checks the password and saves it on this computer, so pushes and backups work. The story map stays locked for everyone else. storymaps unlock [target] [-f <path>] [--remove] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from. Needed in a project folder. --remove Take the lock off for everyone. storymaps unlock storymaps unlock --remove Backs up the story map on the server, or every story map in a project with the same note. Makes no new backup if nothing changed since one of them. See Back up and restore from the terminal. storymaps backup [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] [-m <note>] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from, for one story map. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. -m, --message <note> A note, to tell the backup apart later. storymaps backup storymaps backup -m "Before the release" Lists the backups of the story map, newest first, with the ID to restore each one by. In a project, the newest backup of each story map. storymaps backups [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from, for one story map. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. storymaps backups Puts one story map back to a backup, after backing it up as it is now. Changes the story map, not your file, so pull afterwards. In a project folder, the backup ID says which story map. storymaps restore <backup-id> [target] [-f <path>] [--dir <folder>] [--force] backup-id The ID of the backup, from storymaps backups. -f, --file <path> The file to read the story map from. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --force Restore without asking first. storymaps restore 2d61dc7cf364 Checks a YAML or JSON story map file, or every story map file in a folder, without the server. See Validate and convert story map files. storymaps validate <file or folder> storymaps validate storymap.yml storymaps validate storymaps Turns a story map file from YAML into JSON, or from JSON into YAML. storymaps convert <file> [--from <format>] [--to <format>] [--out <file>] --from <format> yaml or json. Worked out from the file name if left out. --to <format> yaml or json. yaml if left out. --out <file> The file to write. Prints in the terminal if left out. storymaps convert storymap.yml --to json storymaps convert coffee.json --out coffee.yml Starts a project, with a first story map or one from each file, written to the storymaps folder. See Start a project from the terminal. storymaps project init [--name <name>] [files...] [--dir <folder>] [-s <site>] --name <name> The project name. Untitled project if left out. files Story map files to start from. They're left as they are. --dir <folder> Where to write the story maps. storymaps if left out. -s, --site <site> The server to make it on. storymaps.io if left out. storymaps project init --name "Coffee shop" storymaps project init --name "Coffee shop" app.yml barista.yml Adds a story map to the project: a new one, one from a file, or one that already exists. Works offline: the next push creates it. storymaps project add [file or link] [--name <name>] [--dir <folder>] [--project <link>] file or link A story map file, or a story map by its link or ID. A new blank story map if left out. --name <name> The name of a new story map. My Story Map if left out. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --project <link> The project, when there's no project folder yet. storymaps project add --name "Barista Screen" storymaps project add storymaps.io/abc12345 Locks the project, or the project and its story maps, the same two choices as in the app. See Lock and unlock a project. storymaps project lock [--maps] [--yes] [--dir <folder>] [--project <link>] --maps Lock the story maps that aren't locked too, without asking. On a locked project, lock only those. -y, --yes Take the usual answer: the project alone. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --project <link> The project, when there's no project folder. storymaps project lock storymaps project lock --maps Unlocks the project on this computer, or takes its lock off for everyone. storymaps project unlock [--remove] [--maps] [--yes] [--dir <folder>] [--project <link>] --remove Take the lock off for everyone. --maps Also unlock the story maps that use the project password, or with --remove, take their locks off. -y, --yes Take the usual answers: the project only, and the story map locks kept. --dir <folder> The project folder. storymaps if left out. --project <link> The project, when there's no project folder. storymaps project unlock storymaps project unlock --remove --maps

title: User story mapping for developers
description: Pull a user story map as YAML with the Storymaps CLI, hand it to an AI coding agent as the spec, or self-host the open source user story mapping tool.

headings.text: Your story map, in your repo
A spec your agent can read and update
Run it on your own server

text: The same user story map your team plans in, from your terminal, your AI coding agent and your own server. Script it. Pull a story map or a whole project into YAML, change it next to your code, and push it from your terminal or CI. Build with an agent. Hand the story map to Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI as the spec, and it builds a slice at a time. Host it yourself. Open source under AGPL-3.0. One Docker container behind Caddy, with HTTPS set up for you and no analytics. Your story map, in your repo. Pull a story map as YAML, change it alongside your code, check what changed and push it back. Everyone with the story map open sees the change straight away. One story map, two views. The story map in the browser and the file in your repo are the same thing. A card marked done in the file is done on the story map. The plan changes with the code. Commit the story map next to the feature. Reviewers see which cards a change finishes, and storymaps push sends it once it's merged, from your terminal or CI. A spec your agent can read and update. Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI read the story map as the plan and build a slice at a time. Ask the agent to add cards or mark what shipped as done, and it edits the file and pushes. The team sees it in the browser. Run it on your own server. Storymaps.io is an open source user story mapping tool, under AGPL-3.0. It's one Docker container behind Caddy, with HTTPS set up for you, and a self-hosted copy sends no analytics. The CLI works with it the same way: give it your site once. Every story map is data. Add .json, .yaml or .csv to the end of any story map link for its data, always as it is right now. There's no export step and nothing to keep in sync. pull / push: Sync a story map or a whole project diff: See what changed before you push status / log: Progress by slice, and every change lock / unlock: Keep an agreed plan as it is backup / restore: Save a version, and go back to it validate / convert: Check a file in CI, YAML to JSON and back
